Inuocatione manifes ita necromantici et mulierculae, quas vulgo maleficas nuncupamus, miranda faciũt: qui similitudine voluntatis deprauati in consor tium daemonum transierũt. Nam ficut in ec clesia dei sacramenta signa sunt gratiae inuis ibilis spiritus sanctitita in schola daemonior rum characteres quidam et inuocatiũ mo di notae sunt pacti hominis et spiritus malis gni. QUAESTIO TERTIA. gai. Vnde maleficiis daemonum signa praefrentibus maligni spiritus inuocati libenter consueuerunt occurrere: & horrenda maleficia simul et miranda quaedam exhibere. Sed aliter maleficiae atque aliter necromantici daemonum inuocatione mirandos producunt effectus. Maleficiae quodam professionis generis subiiciuntur daemonibus, quorum ministerio aerem turbant, tempestates fuscitae, fruges deuastant, homines et iumenta infirmant. Agunt cum daemonibus spurcissimae voluptatis foeda commertia, & eos pernitio fiscarminibus quos voluerint ab inferis res vocant in aspectum. Harum facta non miracula sed potius maleficia dicenda sunt, & extremo supplicio merito punienda. Necromantici vero non professione manifesta, sed implicita conditione daemonibus se subiiciunt, dum eos non solum coniurationibus et ostensione characterum, sed etiam sacrificiis, fumigis, & votis ad circulum viuibles compellere pollicentur. Horum infinita sunt scelera, quoniam in consortium daemonum vel implicite vel explicite omnes conspirare manifestamet. Quamuis autem necromantici non omnes vel arte vel opere sint pares, in perniciem ramen propriam dam: IOH. TRITTEN. ABB. SPAN. damnabili curiositate omnes sunt concors destqua daemonum suffragio cupiunt asseq, quod naturaliter nequeunt inuenire. Omnia eorum et opera et volumina superstitionibus et impietate sunt plena, & ob id procul à finibus credentium exterminanda. Magna incaetatorum et necromanticorum in oriente multitudine est, qui suis praestigiis humanum genus miserabiliter decipiunt: & pene totam Asiam maiorem et minorem à fide Christi dudum auerterunt. Tribus modis fieri praestigia possunt, ministerio daemonum, opera tione naturae, & deceptione artis humanae. Miracula infidelium vno istorum fieri modo nullus dubitat verus Christianorum ubi radix ponitur determinata operantis. Sunt autê hodie cõplures inter Christianos demonum operibus dediti, incantatores, ma lefici, & reprobi circa fidet qui multos nimia curiositate decipiunt et suis artibus impossibi a promittunt: Implicatione vero daemonum quandoque fiunt miranda, quotiens vis delicet homo non satis recte in fide firmatus aliquid operatur vel optat alique decet Chris tianum:etiam fi nullum credit eë pecccatũ: quod cum fieri non debeat, nihilominus dia bolus se intromiscens optatum plerũque prae stat

when miracles occur by the merit of the sufferer alone, just as we read that many were healed by bad Christians whom the sick believed to be excellent in faith. Third, there is no doubt that such healings occur by the merit of both, that is, of the sufferer and of the worker together, as Christ says to someone in the holy Gospel: If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes. For faith is so necessary for a miracle that our Lord Jesus Christ, when he came into his own country, marveled because he could not do any mighty work there because of their unbelief. But none of these things takes place among unbelievers, where neither holiness is found in the worker nor orthodox faith in the sufferer.

Therefore, third, a man works miracles through the cooperation of the devil out of wickedness. And this can happen in three ways: by manifest invocation of demons, by implicit involvement, and by substitution. By manifest invocation, necromancers and the little women whom we commonly call witches do wondrous things; corrupted by likeness of will, they have passed into fellowship with demons. For just as in the church of God the sacraments are signs of the invisible grace of the Holy Spirit, so in the school of demons certain characters and modes of invocation are tokens of a pact between a man and a malignant spirit.

Hence, when sorceries bear the signs of demons, the malignant spirits invoked are accustomed readily to come, and to display horrible sorceries and at the same time certain wondrous things. But witches and necromancers produce wondrous effects by the invocation of demons in different ways. Witches are subjected to demons by a certain kind of profession; by their ministry they disturb the air, raise storms, lay waste crops, and make men and beasts sick. They carry on foul dealings of the filthiest lust with demons, and by destructive spells call back from the underworld into sight whomever they wish. Their deeds should not be called miracles, but rather sorceries, and they deserve to be punished with the ultimate penalty.

Necromancers, however, subject themselves to demons not by manifest profession but by implicit condition, when they promise to compel them to appear visibly in a circle not only by conjurations and the display of characters, but also by sacrifices, fumigations, and vows. Their crimes are infinite, since it is clear that they all conspire into fellowship with demons, either implicitly or explicitly. And although necromancers are not all equal either in art or in work, nevertheless, to their own destruction, they are all united in damnable curiosity, because they desire to attain by the help of demons what they cannot discover naturally. All their works and volumes are full of superstitions and impiety, and for that reason they must be driven far from the borders of believers.

There is a great multitude of enchanters and necromancers in the East, who miserably deceive the human race by their illusions and long ago turned almost all Asia, both Greater and Lesser, away from the faith of Christ. Illusions can be produced in three ways: by the ministry of demons, by the operation of nature, and by the deception of human art. No true Christian doubts that the miracles of unbelievers occur in one of these ways, when the definite root of the worker is established.

Today, moreover, there are many among Christians devoted to the works of demons: enchanters, witches, and men reprobate concerning the faith, who deceive many by excessive curiosity and promise impossibilities by their arts. By implicit involvement of demons, however, wondrous things sometimes occur whenever, that is, a man not sufficiently and rightly grounded in the faith does or desires something other than befits a Christian, even if he does not believe it to be any sin; and although this ought not to happen, nevertheless the devil, intruding himself, often supplies the desired thing.

15
QUAESTIO TERTIA. stat effectum. Tale nang est illud quo spa lmatici plerumq vtuntur. In die sacro paraf ceues annulum cuiuscũ metalli sub officio fabricant:quem semper postea in digito cor diali portant. Vanifflma fuit hec, nullam pe nitus radicem veritatis habentia. Attamẽ vi diffe me quosdam eadem vanitate curatos à spalmo negare non possum. Item verbis et herbis fortifflmas quosdam aperuiffe feras mihi constattquod neq dei virtute neq vio lentia rerum appositarum existimo factum. Innumera quaae vidi et audiui, possem intro ducere similia:quorum effectus manifesti qd funt aliud,quam quaedam daemonum mira cula. Sunt deniq nonnulli homines nimiũ curiosi,qui characteribus, schedulis, annulis figuris monilibusq, & vocabulis ignotis fi dem et confidentiam pertinaciter adhibẽtes mirandos saepe consequuntur effectus:quos neq sanctitatis merito, neq dei cõceslos mi feratione,fed perfida potius credulitate sub miniftraffe diabolum minime dubitamus. Daemones enim maximam humani generis inuidiam habentes, vt animas perdant mor t alium,libenter occurrunt vanis operationi bus impiorum. Quid nam fuit aliud chara ceres,&occultorum interpretationes nomi minum JOH. TRIT. ABB. SPAN. numi quam eculenta quaedam et potagia daemonior. Quicũq characterib mirabiles effectus pmittetibus fidē adhibet, & fidē chri et ecclesiam fanctorum implicite negauit. Heu quot hodie Christiani, quot celerici, quot sacerdotes (vt maioribus parcam) superstitiis bus et multis et varijs vtuntur in actionibus quotidianis: quibus implicitas daemoniae quantur pactiones, in contumeliam Christi anae fidei et propriam condemnatioem. Ec quia haec mala iam nimium sunt inter Christianos multiplicata, retraxit omnipotens ma num, & tradidit eos in ditionem perfidioris vt exactores poenarum illos sentiant, quoe imitatione non deo viuo et vero, fed vanis superstitionibus pertinaciter militabat. Sup positione autem daemonum miranda fieri manifeste cognoscemus, si diligentius veritatem inquirimus. Iudaei nanci Sarracaeni, pagani, sive gentiles, qui non credunt in deum nostrum Iesum Christum, si qua faciunt miracula, non dei virtute, non agelorum ministerio, non sanctitatis merito, fed daemonum credimus suppositione facta. Nam quotiens omnipotentem deum, in cuius vnigenitum filium non credunt, pro alicuius mirandi effectus miferatione inuocant: scens diabolus q̄ QUAESTIO TERTIA, quoniam non est peccatoribus salus, & quia Psalteri non exaudit altissimus peccatores infideles: Iohannes vt eos in erroribus conseruet pertinaces, se occulte pro deo inuocato applicat: & si pot, permittente domino, quod postulatur orati tibus praestat. Hac diabolus suppositio tan to liberius vitur, quanto minus à fide Christi et Ecclesiae sacramentis impeditur. Manet emira dei super omnes infideles, qui non cre dunt in eius vnigenitum filium: & sunt i po testate diaboli, acideo se inuocantibus inge rie loco dei. Vnde in suis erroribus obcaecati deum inuocant, in cuius filium non credunt quos in ira manetes audire cum delpicit, falsi miraculorum operator diabolus accedit credunt ergo ludificationibus diaboli, q cre dere contemnunt veris miraculis dei. A daemonibus falsa miracula suis convenientia er roribus accipiuntq veritatem. i. Christu, seg credendo noluerunt. Multi sunt enim apud ist deles, q vnum deum creatori omniu colent tes, idola nō adorant et firmi credunt i sua se fi de saluados. Vng q a mysteriis dnicae icarna tiõis credere delpiciat, manet sup eos ira dei, & i suis fatuitatib eu anescuntexifimantes si bi deũ eẽ pximũ, i que nō recte credunt, subnct unt daemõibus: qre falsis miraculis fide adhi bẽres

Such, for instance, is the thing that those afflicted with spasms commonly use. On the holy day of Parasceve they make a ring of some metal during the office, and thereafter they always wear it on the heart-finger. These are utterly vain things, having no root at all in truth. Yet I cannot deny that I have seen some people cured of spasm by that same vanity. Likewise, I know that certain people have opened the strongest locks by words and herbs, which I do not think was done either by the power of God or by the force of the things applied.

I could bring forward countless similar things that I have seen and heard; their manifest effects are nothing other than certain marvels of demons. Finally, there are some overly curious people who stubbornly put faith and confidence in characters, little written sheets, rings, figures, necklaces, and unknown words, and often obtain astonishing effects. We do not doubt at all that the devil supplied these, not through any merit of holiness, nor by God’s merciful grant, but rather through faithless credulity.

For demons, having the greatest envy of the human race, gladly assist the vain works of the impious in order to destroy the souls of mortals. For what else were characters and interpretations of hidden names but certain foods and drinks of demons? Whoever puts faith in characters that promise marvelous effects has implicitly denied both the faith of Christ and the Church of the saints. Alas, how many Christians today, how many clerics, how many priests, to say nothing of their superiors, use many and various superstitions in their daily actions, by which implicit pacts with demons are entered into, to the insult of the Christian faith and to their own condemnation.

And because these evils have now multiplied too much among Christians, the Almighty has withdrawn his hand and handed them over to the power of the faithless, so that they may feel them as exactors of punishments, since by imitation they were stubbornly serving not the living and true God but vain superstitions.

That marvelous things are done by the substitution of demons we shall clearly recognize if we inquire more diligently into the truth. Jews, Saracens, pagans, or gentiles, who do not believe in our God Jesus Christ, if they perform any miracles, we believe that they are done not by the power of God, not by the ministry of angels, not by the merit of holiness, but by the substitution of demons. For whenever they invoke almighty God, in whose only-begotten Son they do not believe, for the merciful granting of some marvelous effect, the devil, knowing that there is no salvation for sinners, and that the Most High does not hear unbelieving sinners, secretly applies himself in place of the God invoked, so that he may keep them stubborn in their errors; and, if he can, with the Lord permitting it, he grants to their prayers what is asked.

The devil uses this substitution all the more freely, the less he is hindered by the faith of Christ and the sacraments of the Church. For the wrath of God remains upon all unbelievers who do not believe in his only-begotten Son; and they are in the power of the devil, and therefore he thrusts himself upon those who invoke them in place of God. Hence, blinded in their errors, they invoke God, in whose Son they do not believe; and when he disdains to hear them while they remain under wrath, the devil, the false worker of miracles, comes near. Thus they believe the devil’s deceptions, while they scorn to believe the true miracles of God. From demons they receive false miracles suited to their errors, because they have refused to believe the truth, that is, Christ.

For there are many among the unbelievers who worship one God, the creator of all things, do not adore idols, and firmly believe that they will be saved in their own faith. But because they disdain to believe the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation, the wrath of God remains upon them; and they vanish away in their follies, thinking God near to them, while, since they do not believe rightly, they are subjected to demons. Therefore, putting faith in false miracles...

16
IOH. TRIT. ABBA. SPAN. bentes in suis erroribus mendacio confirmatur. Cuius rei similitudine introduxisse o Ce far non pidgeat: Erat homo quidã custos por corum, qui schedulã bacillo incluserat nomé diui martyris Blasii continentemt cui tatum fidei detulit, vt baculo in medio gregis terre affixo lupum ab accessu phibitum crederet omnem. Hac ftulta confidentia per longam experientiam tandem roborata, ibat hõ secu rus quocung volebat, dimittens sine pericu lo in nemore porcos cum luporum iã nullus haberet accessum. Contigit pertranfire vidẽ tem absente pastore, qui cernẽs daemōem cu stodia habere gregis, dixit ad eum: Quid mi ferhic agis? Qui respondit: Istos custodio' por cos. At ille: Quis tibi curam porcorum com misit? Iterum respondit: Stulta confidentia pastoris. Nam schedulam quandam bacillo, inclusam magnae putat esse virtutis, qua Bla si cuiusdam meritis lupi arceantur à porcise suam peccavit in legem, & nostras sequit va nitates. Verum quia inuocatus non compa ret, ego ne homo confidentiam suam amitte ret, porcos eius custodio: & me pro Blasio li bẽs suppono. Ita, inquit, mortales vanis cõu ratiõibus nos molestât, vt nĩ velimus aesti matiõem nĩ et honorẽ apud eos pdere, oẽm necel QUAESTIO TERTIA. necesse fit vt corruocatiõibus stultis plerũq soccurramus. Huius similitudine faeti daemo nes miseros infideles decipiunt, & miracula quae orătes à deo postulant, malignior spiris tuum suppositione saepius affequitur. In his enim quae dei vel cultum respiciunt vel hono rem,libenter se daemões ingerũt,& qui mani festos honores affequi nequnt, occultis nimi rum delectâtur. Simul notādum, & ab initio müdi nulli vnq religiõivel sectae pricipaliter excellēti defuere miraculat quamuis nō om nia ex vno principio sint facta. Nam quic quid miraculorum in veta religiõe faciũ est nō aliũde quam àdeo factum est. Habuit em lex naturae miracula sua, habuit lex scripta, habuit iam simul et gratia. Qui religionem dedit omnipotens deus, ipfe etiam miracula facit. In falis autem religionibus, vbi veritas non colitur, fi qua fiunt miracula, non deus fed diabolus operatur. Deus enim cum sitve ritas,religiones falsas non inftituit: & ideo fuis miraculis nunquam médacium illustrat uit. Machumet qui malo daemoe plenus fal fam religionem inftituit,non ex deo fed cos operatione daemonum falsis eam miraculis exornauit. Demon etenim qui caufam de dit erroris,etiam miraculũ,occathioe th accepta D fals IOH. TRIT. ABB. SPAN. falsum potuit exhibere deceptis. Vnde si Ma humeto nouam religionem rudi populo per suadenti penitus defuissent miracula, nemo ei forsita adhibuisset fidem. Ostendit enim Xipe tam subtilitate ingenii quam coopera tione diaboli quaedam miranda populis, vt nouam doctrinam nouis quocq miraculis confirmasse videretur. Paganis idololatris etiam non defuerunt miracula, si fidem histo riis non negamus. Iudaei vero ante incarnas tionem filij dei legem eius fuscipientes pMo sen divinis frequenter miraculis fuerunt illu strati. At vero post dominicam resurrectio nem euacuata lege Mosaica, qui non credunt in vnigenitum filium dei, manent sub ira in dignationis eius: & cessauerunt ab eis oia mi racula veritatis. Vnde si qua hodie miranda faciunt, daemōum sunt opera, & manifesti in dicia erroris. Maximo enim daemōes studio inuigilant, vt eos homines quos à via verita tis quae Christus est, semel fecerunt errantes, continuatione fraudis vscq ad mortem faci ant in errore pertinaces. Enimuero cum de us gratiam suam infidelibus iusta ratiõe sub trahit, eorum deceptor malignus spiritus in cognitus accedit: & quilonge salutem abesse conspicit, falsis miraculis quasi ppefit domi nus,

Those who believe are confirmed in their errors by a lie. To illustrate this matter, let it not be irksome to introduce a comparison.

There was a certain man, a keeper of pigs, who had enclosed in a staff a little written slip containing the name of the holy martyr Blasius. He put so much faith in it that, when the staff was fixed in the ground in the midst of the herd, he believed every wolf to be barred from approaching. When this foolish confidence had at last been strengthened by long experience, the man went wherever he wished in security, leaving the pigs in the wood without danger, since no wolf now had any access to them.

It happened, while the shepherd was absent, that a certain man with sight passed by; seeing that a demon had charge of the herd, he said to him, “Wretch, what are you doing here?” He answered, “I am guarding these pigs.” The other said, “Who entrusted you with the care of the pigs?” He answered again, “The shepherd’s foolish confidence. For he thinks that a certain slip enclosed in a staff has great power, by which, through the merits of some Blasius, wolves are kept away from the pigs; he has sinned against his own law and follows our vanities. But because the one invoked does not appear, I, lest the man lose his confidence, guard his pigs, and willingly put myself in Blasius’s place.” “Thus,” he said, “mortals trouble us with vain conjurations, so that, unless we wish to lose our reputation and honor among them, we must very often come to the aid of foolish invocations.”

In a likeness of this fact, demons deceive wretched unbelievers, and the miracles that they ask of God when they pray are quite often obtained by the substitution of a more malignant spirit. For in matters that concern either the worship or the honor of God, demons willingly thrust themselves in; and since they cannot obtain open honors, they are of course delighted with hidden ones.

At the same time it must be noted that, from the beginning of the world, miracles of special excellence have never been lacking to any religion or sect, although not all have been done from one principle. For whatever miracles have been done in the true religion have been done from no other source than God. The law of nature had its miracles; the written law had its miracles; and now grace likewise has its miracles. The almighty God who gave religion also performs miracles. But in false religions, where truth is not worshiped, if any miracles are done, it is not God but the devil who works them. For since God is truth, he does not establish false religions, and therefore he has never adorned a lie with his miracles.

Muhammad, who, filled with an evil demon, established a false religion, adorned it with false miracles not from God but by the cooperation of demons. For the demon who gave the cause of error could also, when the occasion was taken, display a false miracle to the deceived. Hence, if miracles had been wholly lacking to Muhammad as he persuaded an uncultivated people to a new religion, perhaps no one would have put faith in him. For he too, both by the subtlety of his mind and by the cooperation of the devil, showed certain wonders to the peoples, so that he might seem to have confirmed a new doctrine also by new miracles.

Miracles were not lacking even to pagan idolaters, if we do not deny the histories. The Jews, however, before the incarnation of the Son of God, receiving his law through Moses, were frequently illumined by divine miracles. But after the Lord’s resurrection, when the Mosaic law had been made void, those who do not believe in the only-begotten Son of God remain under the wrath of his indignation, and all miracles of truth have ceased among them. Hence, if they perform any wonders today, they are the works of demons and manifest signs of error. For demons keep watch with the greatest zeal so that those men whom they have once made to wander from the way of truth, which is Christ, they may, by continuing their fraud, make obstinate in error even unto death. Indeed, when God for just reason withdraws his grace from unbelievers, their deceiver, the malignant spirit, approaches unrecognized; and when he sees that salvation is far away, he presents himself by false miracles as though he were the Lord present.

17
QUAESTIO TERTIA. nus, mentes ignorantium seducit. Demonis igitur sunt opera quaecunque infidelium miracula, quoniam sicut extra unitatem Christiae fidei nōt est salus mortalibus sita sine christo non conceditur mirabilium sanctissima virtus. Nunc etenim daemones in insidias lastitātes, tropheo Christi dudū victi atq̄ cōfusi, in apto cōparere vt a[n] incarnatiōne dñi me tuũt et ideo se apd ifideles p bonis spiritib. mēdaci[?] ostēdũt. Sũt etiā q̄ pscriptis tribũmodis adiçiũt qrtũ, dicētes mētẽ hue spiritũ is pũ[?] hois posse naturaliter miranda facere s modo sciat se ab omni aduētitio in seipsum supra sensum in unitatem reuocare. Pollicẽtur enim, qui talia a[?]truunt, naturae mirāda facere, futura praedicere, secreta hominũ pādere, morbos auferre, & hominum subito consilia immutare. Sed ifte miraculorum modus non potest esse simpliciter naturalis, certus, communis et infallibilis: quoniam si verus est (quod ego non sum expertus) necel[?] le eft iam aliquid externae potestatis occurre[?] re: & vel angelum bonum, vel spiritum ma[?] lignum, cogitantem in parte occupare. Si autem nihil exterarum virtutum se itermis[?] cet, necesse est vaticinantem vel ex coniectu[?] ris vel ex audaci plumptione loqndi forma IOH. TRITTEN. ABB. SPAN. re principium: & aliquando verum aliqndo falsum pronuntiare iudiciũ. Enimuero quãs diu versatur in corpore spiritus, nihil natura liter intelligit sine ministerio sensus. Vñ non obniterer penitus, si confusum et rudẽ intellectum nostrum pari cõcedant ministerio ad iuuari. Cernimus enim in his qui plerũque a moris interni ad lesum defiderio carnis mo dum contemplantes excedũt, à terra fursum levatos in aera: quos non sua duntaxat acie mentis, sed divina nihilominus virtute pons dus excedere corporale putamus. Tria igit memoratẽ opinionis principia incognita mul tis, satisfaciunt mea sententia paucis, vt mẽ in corpore posita mirandos extra se propria virtute operetur effectus. Quid enim? Dicat mihi nature quisquis ignarus, vtrum corpo rale pondus operatione mentis alleuiari po fit? Ego contestantibus mecum duobus rem dico expertam. Cum prosequeret adolelçẽ studia literarum, in vno lecto quatuor erã mus nocte quadam dormientes. Surrexit e latere meo coaeuus et dormiẽs, vt solebat, in omnis domum oculis clausis et luna intro lucente quintadecima quafi vigil circumam bulabat. Ascẽdit muros, & aelurum agilitate suavincebat. Tectum quoque secũdo et tectio lopi QUAESTIO TERTIA. Sopitus transcendit, calcauit nos pedibus oes nec magis sensimus podus, quā si mus nos contigisset exiguus. Quocung dormiēs cor pus mouebatur, subito ianuarum omnes vi tro aperiebantur clausurae. Altiora domus edificia velociflme penetravit, & more pas ceris haerebat in tectis. Vīsa loquor non vas ga relatione audita. Haec animae non corpo ris videntur officia quae sua naturali potesta te, vt ita dixerim, quasi libere vtitur, quādo ligatis sensibus carnis extra domiciliu cor poris euagatur. Sed cum non sit propositae quaestioni materia ex omni parte conueni eus, de causis horum mirabilium in aliud tempus remittam us tractatum. Haud enim credimus ista miranda sapientibus, qui mē tis humanae virtutem et nobilitatem optime intellexerunt, vt pote qua solo corporis inter iectu remorata, de aliquo par angelis aestis mat. Fascinationũ deniç et varios modos pertrāsimus et genera, quibus ad externa fu riosus valde minādos opatur effectus. Mul ta etiam potest ad producēdos mirabiles ef fectus fortiffime confidentis imaginatio, si ue in verum fiue in aestimatum feratur obie ctum. Vnde cum tot sint operandi miranda et genera et modi, non est mirandum, si lu D 3 daei,

Therefore whatever miracles belong to unbelievers are works of the demon, since, just as there is no salvation for mortals outside the unity of the Christian faith, so without Christ the most holy power of miracles is not granted. For now the demons, long since conquered and confounded by the trophy of Christ, fear to appear openly since the incarnation of the Lord, and therefore among unbelievers they falsely present themselves as good spirits.

There are also some who add a fourth mode to the three already described, saying that the mind, or spirit, of man himself can naturally perform wonders, provided only that it knows how to withdraw itself from every adventitious thing into itself, above sense, into unity. For those who maintain such things promise wonders of nature: to predict the future, disclose men’s secrets, take away diseases, and suddenly alter men’s plans. But this mode of miracles cannot be simply natural, certain, common, and infallible; for if it is true, which I have not experienced, some external power must necessarily intervene, and either a good angel or an evil spirit must in part take possession of the one who is thinking. But if none of the external powers mingles itself within, then the one prophesying must necessarily form the ground of his speech either from conjectures or from bold presumption, and at times pronounce a true judgment, at times a false one.

Indeed, so long as the spirit dwells in the body, it naturally understands nothing without the ministry of sense. Therefore I would not wholly resist them if they grant that our confused and crude understanding is aided by a like ministry. For we see in those who, in contemplation, often pass beyond the measure of the flesh through inward love and desire for Jesus, that they are lifted upward from the earth into the air; and we think that they overcome bodily weight not merely by their own keenness of mind, but also by divine power. Thus the three principles of the opinion mentioned, unknown to many, in my judgment satisfy few, namely that the mind, while placed in the body, should by its own proper power produce wonderful effects outside itself.

For what then? Let anyone ignorant of nature tell me whether bodily weight can be lightened by the operation of the mind. I speak of a thing I experienced, with two others bearing witness with me. When, as a youth, I was pursuing literary studies, four of us were sleeping one night in one bed. A boy of my own age rose from beside me while asleep and, as was his habit, went about the whole house with his eyes closed, while the full moon shone in, almost as if awake. He climbed walls and surpassed the agility of cats. Still asleep, he crossed over the second roof and [unclear], trod on all of us with his feet, and we felt his weight no more than if a little mouse had touched us. Wherever his sleeping body moved, all the fastenings of the doors at once opened of themselves. He passed through the higher parts of the house with the greatest speed, and, like a sparrow, clung upon the roofs.

I speak of things seen, not heard by vague report. These seem to be functions of the soul, not of the body; by its natural power, so to speak, it uses them almost freely when, the senses of the flesh being bound, it wanders outside the dwelling of the body. But since this matter does not in every respect suit the proposed question, I shall defer the treatment of the causes of these marvels to another time. For we do not think these wonders strange to the wise, who have very well understood the power and nobility of the human mind, since, hindered only by the interposition of the body, it is in some respect judged equal to the angels. Finally, we pass over the various modes and kinds of fascinations, by which a mind driven to frenzy works very threatening effects upon external things. The imagination of one who is most strongly confident can also do much toward producing marvelous effects, whether it is directed toward a true object or toward one merely supposed. Hence, since there are so many kinds and modes of working wonders, it is not surprising if Jews,

IOH. TRIT. ABBA. SPAN. daei,Sarracaeni, pagani,geriles,ac relij extra fidem Christi constituti,quicunq infideles, qui facere miracula per publicam iustitiam nequeunt, miranda vel daemōum suffragio vel artificiosa industria committūt. Nec me fugit pari quidem ratione miracula sanctore impugnari ab impiis,quasi non virtute creatores fiant,sed potius implicatiõe vel suppos stiõe diaboli. Quisquis Christianam fidem solam veraciter credit esse veram, omnium infidelium miracula cooperatione demonũ non dubitat esse patrata.Si quis vero contra rium temere et pertinaciter fenserit,infidelẽ te non Christianum ostendit. Descriptura sacra. QUAESTIO QVARTA. Varta vero sereniss.Maiestatis uxe quaestio fuit ista: Quare o mnipotẽs deus scripturam san tam noui quàm veteris estamẽi mysteria fidei nostrae continentem,non dederit apertam,manife stam in omnibusq vuniformem et palam ad omnia sufficientem: sed inuolutam potius, & in QUAESTIO QVARTA. & in multis locis enigmatibus plenam. Multa enim ad perfectiorem fidei sunt necessaria quae in divinis scripturis non reperiuntur sufficienter expressa. Ad hanc Maiestatis tuae sacra tissima questionem videtur respondendum: Omnis scriptura divinitus inspirata perfectum divinitatis est opus ante tempus omne prae ordinatum, in tempore scriptum, non secus quam Deus voluit, qui ut scriberetur homini bus inspirauit. Dei autem omnia perfecta sunt opera, ideoque cum scriptura de qua lo quimur dei sit opus, necessarium est eam in omnibus confiteri perfectam. Summus ete nim arbiter Deus, cuius omnia perfecta sunt opera, sicut voluit et quae voluit scripturis suis ordiné contulit: & excipientibus illas quae admodum scriberent, proculdubio infudit. Sacra neque scripturae tantam omnipotens Deus authoritatem et maiestatem contulit, vt in eius comparatione omnia huius mundi vocabula deficiant: cum divina humanis propriae nequeant comprehendendi sermonibus. Divina igitur scriptura quae superficie versibus nescientibus appareat confusa, scientibus eam videtur manifestatq̄n nisi legat illo spiritu quo infusa hominibus creditur, ad esse ipsum intellectum minime peruenitur. Alis D 4 ter JOH. TRIT. ABB. SPAN. ter eam legit doctus q carnis vmbraculo ac vanis defideris aestuat: & aliter intelligens, quem exutum voluptatibus amor dei veraci ter inflammat. Vnde mirum nō est, si homi- nes carnaliter sapiētes divinas scripturas nō intelligent, qui carnis voluptatibus obcecati dei spiritus dulcedinem nūquam preceperūt Quemadmodum si puero prima literarum elementa discenti volumē exhibeas quodcū scriptum, cuius character suo sit libello dis similis, cum legere nequiverit, scripturam ili co malam et non recte formatam exclamas bit. Pari modo ad lectionem diuinarum scri pturarum accedentes homines carnaliter dū taxat sapiētes, qui ea quae diuini spiritus sunt non capiunt, vitis et temeritate graviati cu suam ignorantiām et indignitatem culpāre debuisserit, scripturas, quas non intelligunt, sanctas reprehendunt. Jews, Saracens, pagans, gentiles, and others placed outside the faith of Christ, whatever unbelievers they may be, who cannot perform miracles through public righteousness, carry out wonders either by the aid of demons or by artful skill. Nor am I unaware that by the same argument the miracles of the saints are attacked by the impious, as though they were not done by the power of the Creator, but rather by the involvement or substitution of the devil. Whoever truly believes that the Christian faith alone is true does not doubt that all the miracles of unbelievers have been performed by the cooperation of demons. But if anyone rashly and stubbornly thinks the contrary, he shows himself to be an unbeliever, not a Christian.

On Sacred Scripture.

The fourth question of your most serene Majesty was this: why almighty God did not give holy Scripture, containing the mysteries of our faith in both the New and the Old Testament, open, manifest, uniform in all things, and plainly sufficient for everything, but rather wrapped up and, in many places, full of riddles. For many things necessary for the fuller perfection of faith are not found sufficiently expressed in the divine Scriptures.

To this most sacred question of your Majesty it seems that this answer should be given: every Scripture inspired by God is a perfect work of divinity, ordained before all time, written in time, in no other way than God willed, who inspired men that it should be written. But all the works of God are perfect; and therefore, since the Scripture of which we speak is the work of God, it is necessary to confess that it is perfect in all things. For God, the supreme judge, whose works are all perfect, conferred upon his Scriptures, in order, what he willed and as he willed; and he undoubtedly infused into those who received them what they were to write.

Nor did almighty God give to sacred Scripture such authority and majesty that, in comparison with it, all the words of this world would not fail, since divine things cannot properly be comprehended by human speech. Therefore divine Scripture, which on the surface of its verses appears confused to the ignorant, seems clear to those who know it; and unless one reads it in that Spirit by which it is believed to have been infused into men, one by no means reaches its true understanding.

The learned man who burns under the shadow of the flesh and with vain desires reads it in one way; the man whom the love of God truly inflames, stripped of pleasures, understands it in another. Hence it is no wonder if men who think carnally do not understand the divine Scriptures, since, blinded by the pleasures of the flesh, they have never perceived the sweetness of the Spirit of God.

It is just as if you were to show to a boy learning the first elements of letters some written volume whose script was unlike that of his own little book: when he could not read it, he would at once cry out that the writing was bad and not properly formed. In the same way, men who approach the reading of the divine Scriptures while thinking only carnally, and who do not grasp the things that belong to the Spirit of God, weighed down by faults and by rashness, although they ought to have blamed their own ignorance and unworthiness, reproach the holy Scriptures because they do not understand them.

For it is not lawful for everyone indiscriminately to interpret the divine Scriptures, lest the beast that touches the mountain be overwhelmed with stones. Now many arise, in a perverse order, who have spent the whole time of their life on humane letters, and when they have become old men, by wrongly interpreting the divine Scriptures which they have never learned, they do not unfold them but confound them, and examine them according to their own meaning. FOURTH QUESTION

Whoever does not understand the sacred Scriptures in the spirit in which they were infused into their writers has the veil of ignorance and rashness spread over his heart, after the manner of the Jews, and very often drinks in the poison of pernicious error from the place where the humble, approaching in the spirit of God, have received the cup of salvation.

For heavenly doctrine lies not in the words of Scripture, but in the meaning; not on the surface of the sayings, but in the understanding; not in the mere adornment of polished speech, but in the hidden mystery of divine inspiration.

Hence blessed Pope Gregory says: “Sacred Scripture far surpasses all the sciences of this world in the manner of its speech, because in one and the same discourse, while it narrates the text, it reveals a hidden mystery; and just as it refreshes the simple on the surface, so it exercises the wise by its mystery. For it has in public what may nourish little ones, and it preserves in secret what may hold the minds of the lofty suspended in wonder at its sweetness, like some wonderful river in which both the simple little lamb may walk and the great elephant may swim.”

And Saint Augustine says on Genesis: “Divine Scripture speaks in such a way that by its height it mocks the proud, by its depth it terrifies the attentive, by its power it feeds the great, and by its affability it nourishes little ones.”

For the authority of sacred Scripture is greater than all the insight of human intelligence. Therefore, in order to arrive at its true understanding, the mind must first be cleansed of every carnal affection, and the help of divine goodness must be earnestly implored with humility, that by his Spirit he may enlighten the understanding of the learner. For to the authority of the divine Scriptures the necks of all powers must be bowed. And as blessed Jerome says: “No man must ever be flattered in such a way that the truth of the holy Scriptures is neglected”; for in both Testaments it is wholly true in its narration of deeds, right in its admonitions, certain in its promises, and terribly to be feared in its threats.

Therefore it is not given to all to be able to penetrate the mysteries of the divine Scriptures, but this is permitted only to those in whom love makes study continual, and to whose purified minds the Spirit of God grants true understanding. But whoever is soiled by the darkness of vices, whoever walks proudly with a swollen mind, whoever doubts the truth of God’s Scriptures either in part or in whole, should never trust that he can reach an understanding of them. For the authority of Scripture itself says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand.”

It is the slowness of our intelligence, and the impurity of our desire, whenever we do not rightly understand the divine Scriptures; since the veil of pernicious occupation remains spread over our hearts and does not allow us to arrive at true understanding. Hence it comes about that we do not understand the meaning which the Holy Spirit infused into the divine Scriptures, but, grasping only the bare words of the writers, we twist them into another sense.

Indeed, if our minds were cleansed from carnal vices; if, through the continual practice of sobriety, our intelligence were exercised in the Scriptures; if faith and reverence were shown to the holy Scriptures as their dignity requires, every studious person would understand more clearly than light that there is nothing confused in the sacred readings, nothing discordant, nothing unfitting, nothing absurd, nothing inserted without the most just reason.

For every passage of divine Scripture is full of mysteries; and whenever anything in them seems to be set down obscurely, it was done by divine providence, so that the studious mind might have the necessary exercise of devotion, and the faith of the simple might not lose the place of due reverence. Therefore it was not by chance, but by eternal providence, that God wished the holy Scriptures to be obscure in many places, so that they might abound in as many mysteries as meanings, to be explained in a Catholic manner by teachers under the inspiration of the Spirit of God. For, as Augustine says, the obscurity of divine Scripture is very useful.

It is useful and very profitable because it brings forth many true meanings and brings them to light for human beings; when one person draws out this sense, and another draws out another, while expounding it in a catholic way, it becomes known how lofty and deep it is. Therefore no man swollen with secular learning should think that he understands sacred Scripture unless he first lays aside the veil of pride and of every disordered desire. For secular learning is more effective for exercising the intellect than for enlightening the understanding toward true wisdom.

Therefore divine Scripture is, without doubt, clear and bright to minds purified by the continual exercise of the fear of God and by frequent zeal for reading; but to filthy minds, and to those puffed up with secular wisdom, it seems confused and obscure. Hence he understands the holy Scriptures well and rightly who, with purified affection and frequent in the study of them, expounds them as did the one who wrote them. For if they read them in a spirit other than that by which he is believed to have inspired them to be written, the mind must be wholly shut out from the true understanding. But when we encounter some discordance in them, let us understand that it is only of words, not of meanings; and that this arises not by chance, but by the providence of God and in due order, so that the mind, exercised in the Scriptures, may be strengthened the longer and not grow wholly sluggish. For the counsel of God cannot be mistaken; but the divine Scriptures were written according to the counsel of his will. It necessarily follows that they are true and in no way false.

They were human beings by whom the divine Scriptures were handed down to us; certainly they wrote words used according to human custom, by which they might signify to posterity what that supreme excellence of divinity wished to be known to mortals.

Therefore you now, who, devoted to secular wisdom, attack the divine Scriptures, speak: the Scripture of the New and Old Testament, which the Church of Christians has received and venerates as true, authentic, and holy, from where do you believe it was received? From God, or from human beings? If from God, why do you not believe it? For everyone who attacks Scripture, while believing it to be inspired by God, most plainly resists the divine ordering. But if it is from human beings, why do you hope in it for the promised eternal salvation, which a human being cannot give? Unless perhaps, in your madness, you go on to say that all things are fabricated, and that nothing remains after death except ashes, and that the mind perishes together with the body; this profession would show you no less insane than foolish. For if you truly believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, you will necessarily say that the divine Scriptures were inspired by the Holy Spirit. But if, having become apostates into a reprobate mind, you say they were composed by human beings, you impiously show how far you are from true wisdom, wandering in darkness.

You openly show yourselves to be unskilled and rash judges, since you condemn a Scripture that you do not understand. Truly, because it is more familiar to you to despise wisdom than to learn it, it is not the purpose of this work to weary the mind any longer against the rashness of the unskilled. This one thing I want you to know: no one understands unless he receives; but because you place the filth of your affections in the way, so that you may not receive, you therefore do not have the true understanding of wisdom. For almighty God deigns to enlighten by grace those who, stripped of carnal desires, burn with the fire of inward love, who desire nothing in this world except God. The Spirit of God, by his presence, brings help to those whom he finds rooted in the love of truth, and, purified from every foreign thing, he leads them into the knowledge of all things. For truly, to those who love God, all things are open, all things bare, all things manifest; for whoever, through love, beholds in the faith of Jesus Christ the one who creates and governs all things, [unclear] all things that are necessary for his salvation.

knows mysteries. But God’s illumination dwells very far from the slothful, the wicked, gluttons, the envious, the greedy, lechers, the filthy, the lustful, murderers, the impious, the proud, and those estranged from piety, leaving them to the judgment of the avenging demon, who, striking with the sharp point of cruel fire, afflicts sense and mind, and arms and drives the impious still more to commit crimes, so that, guilty of a more shameful fault, they may also become liable to a sharper punishment. Hence, entangled in vices and worldly desires, they not only cannot penetrate the divine Scriptures with understanding, but, neglecting themselves, do not even know themselves.

Since, therefore, sacred Scripture is God’s perfect work, we must so strengthen our mind that we believe it true, right, whole, solid, divinely inspired, and most abundantly sufficient for all who understand it for the confirmation of the Christian faith. For indeed, unless divine Scripture is believed to be true, holy, perfect in all things, and whole, the Christian faith would be deprived of its foundation. Every Christian must therefore take the greatest care lest, by scrutinizing the divine Scriptures more than is fitting, he overstep the bounds of piety; for the author of Scripture is not man, but the Holy Spirit, and whoever struggles against the integrity of God’s Scriptures is convicted of resisting his ordering.

Now Scripture, by God’s ordinance, is beneficially interwoven with parables, riddles, likenesses, and comparisons of figures, so that readers may be exercised toward understanding and, once its inward sweetness has been tasted, the mind may be strengthened toward piety. And so, if with purified minds we attend to the sense of the Scriptures and not to the words alone, we shall understand that all things have been ordered rightly and properly. For it was not fitting that the sacred Scriptures, in which knowledge of the divine majesty is handed down, should be so plain and manifest that they would be understood everywhere by everyone, since they are set forth to be understood only by the good and holy, not also by evil, filthy, and polluted minds.

For this reason it is written: “The beast that touches the mountain shall be stoned.” What is designated here by the beast, except human beings who, in imitation of brute animals, live without the love of God in the pleasures of the flesh? And what is expressed by the mountain, except the height of the divine Scriptures? When the beast approaches this holy mountain, it is overwhelmed with stones, because a person impure in mind, or weak in faith, who attempts to search out the height of the divine Scriptures without a teacher handing it down, is wounded by various and pernicious errors as though by blows of stones. For just as all things are clean to the clean, so all things seem profane to the profane.

God therefore set his hiding place in the height of the Scriptures, which is so inaccessible and closed to the reprobate that it nevertheless always lies plainly open to the saints. But why did almighty God not give holy Scripture as sufficient and manifest for everything that concerns the Christian faith? We answer briefly: there are two things which the Most High provided for believers for the confirmation of the Christian faith, namely the Church and Scripture, so that what is not expressed clearly enough in the one may be declared by the other. Hence, if we find anything in the holy Scriptures expressed less sufficiently concerning the rules of faith, we at once have recourse to the Church; and where the Church has need of saving instruction for piety, it immediately turns to Scripture. From this it follows that neither would the Church have authority without Scripture, nor Scripture faith without the Church, so that from the two one judgment may be made. For Augustine says: “I would not believe the Gospel unless the authority of the Church compelled me.” But John Gerson says: “I would not believe the Church unless the Gospel compelled me.” Sacred Scripture, moreover, confirms

Iium Christi negavit. Vna est fidelium con- gregatio mater Christianorum sancta eccle- sia, extra cuius unitatem nemo saluabit:que et si in moribus quadoque videatur infirma, tamen fide semper constans nunque errauit Christi pietate salua. De reprobis atqz maleficis Quaestio Quinta, Vinta serenissimae Celsitudinis tuae quaestio fuit ista: Quare homines impi, mali, & repro- bi circa fidem, vt sunt illae mulie- res, quas vulgo maleficas nun cupamus, spiritibus queant imperare mali- gnis:ũ viri boni et fidei Christianae studios fissimi observatores, nec bonis spiritib? im- perare possint, nec semp malignis? Ad hanc questione ita me pridẽ memini respondisset In oibus divinae Maiestatis opibus series et ordo pulchritudinis est, immobilis aequitas tis,quo fingula conuenienter disposita,in eo quẽ acceperũt gradu pfeuerũt. Nã fine ordis ne pprio nihil subsistit in mũdo. In hoc ordi ne libertas arbitriũ,quã creator oĩ dedit hoĩ bus,nulla ipelliũ violẽtia potestatis,q minũp E 2 maneat IOHAN. TRIT. ABBA. SPAN. maneat in ordine, quem à principio creationis fuae homo primus acceptit. Vnde nemo bonus inter mortales, nifi propriae consilio voluntatis, adiutus per gratiam miserentis deit et nemo malus, nifi sua sponte gratia destitutus propter obstaculum peccati. Volumetatis autem rectitudine bonis spiritibus effiscimur similes, si pietatem fidei, quam habes mus in Christum, sanctis et necessarijs opes ribus comprobemus. Et sicuti bonae voluntatis consummatio bonos homines spiritibus pares facit angelicis: ita perueritas impiorũ eos similes reddit daemonibus. Vnde mali homines ac peruerși quão amplius malitia propriae voluntatis deprauati fuerint, tanto fiunt daemonibus affectu similiores. Similitudine vero amicitia familiaritas introducitur, ex qua paulatim confidetia mus tua generatur. Ex confidentia minoris in maiorem nascitur imperium, fiue sit verum fiue astutia simulatum. Prauorum itaque hominum si quod imperium esse videtur in daemones, ex magnitudine pruivitatis oritur quado videlicet affectus co et vsqueadeo deprauatur, & concurrentium fibi daemonum malitiam voluntate reproba, vel superant, vel aequant. The Church also, and in like manner, confirms this from Scripture. The Church abounds whenever Scripture falls short; and if anyone has doubts about the Church, he has recourse to the counsel of Scripture. For there is one Holy Spirit of God, who founded the Church in the faith of Jesus Christ, the very same almighty Spirit who alone inspired Scripture. And this is the threefold cord that is not easily broken, where divine Scripture, through the same Spirit, is joined to the authority of the Church, and so prevails that the Church commends Scripture, and Scripture in turn commends the Church.

Therefore, as it seems to me, O Caesar, we have sufficiently assigned the reason for the question proposed by your unconquered Majesty: because, if everything that concerns the piety of faith were plainly expressed in the Holy Scriptures, holy mother Church would not appear to have such great authority, and the merit of saving obedience would in large part be emptied out. At the same time I think enough has been answered to the main question, where certain people suppose that sacred Scripture is in many places confused and entangled; but if they read it with due purity of mind, they would certainly find it perfect and solid. Great is the authority of the Catholic Church, which alone, in doubtful matters concerning the faith, has the right to interpret the Scriptures; to it the necks of all powers must be subjected, and if anyone, with rash daring, departs from its definition, he has denied the Gospel of Christ.

There is one congregation of the faithful, holy Church, the mother of Christians; outside its unity no one will be saved. And although in conduct it may sometimes seem weak, nevertheless, constant always in faith, it has never erred, the loving-kindness of Christ preserving it.

Concerning the reprobate and evildoers

Question Five

The fifth question of your most serene Highness was this: Why can impious, evil, and reprobate people in matters concerning faith, such as those women whom we commonly call witches, command malignant spirits, while good men and the most zealous observers of the Christian faith can command neither good spirits nor always malignant ones?

I remember that I answered this question before in this way. In all the works of the divine Majesty there is a sequence and order of beauty, an unchanging equity, by which each thing, suitably disposed, perseveres in the rank it has received. For without its proper order nothing subsists in the world. In this order the freedom of the will, which the Creator of all gave to all human beings, cannot be compelled by any violence of power not to remain in the order that the first human being received from the beginning of his creation. Hence no one among mortals is good except by the counsel of his own will, aided by the grace of the merciful God; and no one is evil except by his own will, deprived of grace because of the obstacle of sin.

By rectitude of will we are made like the good spirits, if we prove by holy and necessary works the piety of faith that we have in Christ. And just as the perfection of a good will makes good people equal to angelic spirits, so the perversity of the impious makes them like demons. Hence evil and perverse people, the more they have been depraved by the malice of their own will, become so much the more like demons in affection. Through likeness, moreover, friendship and familiarity are introduced, from which little by little mutual confidence is generated. From the lesser’s trust in the greater arises authority, whether it be true or simulated by cunning. Therefore, if there seems to be any authority of wicked people over demons, it arises from the greatness of depravity, namely when their affection is so far depraved, and by their reprobate will they either surpass or equal the malice of the demons that join with them. For demons are not all in malice [unclear].

Duo sunt genera hominum, qui daemonibus imperare licite possunt. Primum quidem illorum est hominum, qui merito sanctitatis deo dilecti potestatem ab ipso conculcandi caput anti qui serpentis acceperunt, quales in Ecclesia primitiva fuerunt apostoli eorumque sequaces atque discipuli, de quibus in sancto Euangelio dominus loquitur: In nomine meo Ma daemonia enicient, & quia serpentes tollent. Secundum vero genus eorum est hominum, quibus ratione ordinis in ecclesia dei conce ditur, ut daemones de hominum corporibus accepti potestate ministerij depellant. Et hoc ministerium exorcistis in ecclesia dei committitur, quando videlicet à Pontifice ordinantur. Rursus sunt duo genera hominum, qui daemonibus imperare cupiunt: quod quam illicite praesumant, iniquissimis conditionibus ostendunt. Primum genus pernitiiosissimum est maleficarum, quae passeta ineunt cum daemonibus, & professione solenni praemissa in ius proprietatis perpetuumque obsequium daemonum alicui semet ipsas tradunt. FIFTH QUESTION

They are not equal in wickedness or intelligence; rather, one is much craftier than another in quickness of understanding, and far worse in corrupt disposition. For those who, having fallen from their high seats, are more closely joined to the earth and inhabit caverns and caves are certainly duller than the rest, to such a degree that they even fear swords and rods, and seem to be moved by the threats of men who terrify them, as may be seen in those whom we call the possessed. But demons who dwell farther from the earth are subtler by nature and encounter human beings more rarely.

Men full of wickedness, however, the more they advance in perversity of will, become so much the more like demons; and, once admitted by them into familiarity, they thereafter grow bold, and acquire a simulated, not truly coercive, authority over demons, which they use by that familiarity. For demons, in order to keep in their own depravity those men whom they have once received into surrender as willing subjects, gladly submit themselves to them, pretending to be moved by their entreaties; and what they do of their own accord they pretend to do as though compelled to obedience.

Indeed no one obtains true authority over demons unless faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, through the merit of holiness, has made him acceptable and a friend to God. For thus Scripture says of those who truly believe in the Lord Jesus: “And he gave them power over all demons.” Therefore evil men command demons because malevolence has made them like them, likeness has made them familiar, and familiarity has made them their own and subject to them.

It is like the case of a great prince, as often happens, if one of his servants, born in a humble station and joined to him by long familiarity, is said to command him, because from him he obtains without contradiction everything he has asked, so that he seems rather to rule his master than to be ruled by him. According to this likeness, evil and reprobate men, who are admitted by demons into close familiarity and become very bold through prolonged confidence, receive over them a simulated, not to say familiar, authority, which they have deserved through the likeness of a most depraved will.

Hence whatever they request from demons, who cooperate with them by an implicit or explicit pact, they receive, unless at times the demons, prevented by divine ordinance, are unable to provide what is asked. Yet demons do not thus cooperate indiscriminately with all reprobate and evil men, but only with those with whom they have entered into alliances through the intervention of some pact: such as witch-women, who have offered homage to the devil, and those invokers of demons whom the common people call by the usual name necromancers.

There are two kinds of men who can lawfully command demons. The first is that of those men who, beloved by God through the merit of holiness, have received from him the power of treading down the head of the ancient serpent, such as in the primitive Church were the apostles and their followers and disciples, of whom the Lord speaks in the holy Gospel: “In my name they shall cast out demons,” and “they shall take up serpents.”

The second kind is that of those men to whom, by reason of order in the Church of God, it is granted to drive demons from the bodies of men by the power of the ministry they have received. And this ministry is committed to exorcists in the Church of God when they are ordained by the bishop.

Again, there are two kinds of men who desire to command demons; and the wicked conditions they accept show how unlawfully they presume to do so. The first and most pernicious kind is that of witches, who enter into pacts with demons and, after making a solemn profession, hand themselves over to some demon as his property and for perpetual service. What great evils this most pernicious kind of human beings commits in your dominion, no one

Mirandum igitur non est, quae maleficia daemonibus imperare videntur, quibus impietate peruersae voluntatis factae sunt familes, & mutua conversatione in malum humani generis concordae. Et quia nos ftris maxime temporibus abundare coepit Iniquitas, & refriguit charitas multorum, isti maledicti ac mendacissimi homies nimium inualuerunt: & quamuis contemnantur à de monibus, nihilominus in suis pernitiosis do gmatibus perseverantes multos decipiunt. Crede mihi Caesar, quoniam hoc mendacis simum genus hominum sacro imperio tuo valde eit pernitiosum: & ideo non minus q maleficarum scaturigo, penitus exterminũ dum. Pollicentur magna, & mentiantur o mnia. Enimuero cuncta que in libris eorum promittuntur, vana sunt et mentita, & nihil praestant credẽtibus aliud, quam dolos, frau des, & subtilissimas deceptiones. Quod fi ŋ do videntur exhibere promissa, non aliter quam daemonum id fieri cooperatione ma nifestum sit omnibus, a quorum consortio non minus est fugendum, quam à saeuissi mis

There is, most wise Caesar, no one who can express it. For, first of all, denying God, the faith of Christ, and holy baptism, they offer themselves in mind and body to demons; by their evil arts they weaken, injure, and kill men and beasts. There is no disease which, if God permits it, they cannot bring on, because, when they present themselves as servants to demons in observance of the covenant contracted with them, in comparison with those spirits they dare whatever they wish.

Therefore they are not to be tolerated at all, but rather are to be utterly exterminated in every place, as God, the creator of all, commands: “You shall not suffer sorcerers to live.” Some witches call upon demons with spells; others entice them with prayers and sacrifices; the rest, provoking them with unspeakable things and ceremonies, draw them into the service of their impiety.

It is therefore not surprising that witches seem to command demons, since through the impiety of a perverse will they have become their servants, and by mutual association are united for the harm of the human race.

The second kind of wicked men who wish to command demons is that of those commonly called necromancers, who profess arts full of abominations, by which they promise that they can summon demons into a circle, or show them openly visible, enclosed in a crystal or some other vessel. These most pernicious men, full of lies and superstitions, commit such evils that no good man could imagine them. For in order to entice demons into their service, they commonly use the foulest sacrifices and enter into an explicit pact with them.

They circulate many various little books full of filth, impiety, and falsehood, deceitfully inscribed with the names of ancient philosophers and sages; by displaying these they deceive many unwary and curious people and drag them with themselves into the pit of demons. They promise great things, indeed things wholly incredible, and by hearing of them they deceitfully hold men suspended in amazement. They say that by rings, pentacles, images, exorcisms, and conjurations they can compel malignant demons to appear visibly in a circle, or in a crystal, or in some other receptacle, and to answer distinctly all questions put to them.

All of them indeed promise this, but in our times very few are found whom malignant spirits, even evil ones, obey in this way, since God, for a most just reason, does not permit it, lest human curiosity, prone to novelties, should despise the religion of Christ and in time of need seek [unclear] assistance from demons. Yet all those whom malignant spirits obey when summoned by the conjurations of necromancers have without doubt passed into their fellowship through an explicit or implicit pact. But the number of the others is greater, whom malignant spirits disdain to obey, although they are not afraid to busy themselves at all times with the profane arts of necromancers.

And because iniquity has begun to abound especially in our times, and the charity of many has grown cold, these accursed and most lying men have become too powerful; and although they are despised by demons, nevertheless, persisting in their pernicious doctrines, they deceive many. Believe me, Caesar, this most deceitful class of men is very harmful to your holy empire, and therefore, no less than the brood of witches, must be utterly exterminated.

They promise great things, and they lie in everything. For in truth all the things promised in their books are empty and false, and they offer those who believe them nothing except tricks, frauds, and the most subtle deceptions. But if at times they seem to present what they have promised, it should be clear to all that this happens only by the cooperation of demons, from whose fellowship one must flee no less than from the most savage [unclear].

QUESTION FIVE.

with the torments of hell. For demons very often appear in these necromantic operations, and, so that they may keep their invokers stubborn in the treachery they have begun, they grant them what is asked, if they can. Sometimes, however, when invoked by conjurations, they disdain to appear, and nevertheless they have led away the minds of those who invoke them.

There is also another kind of people, no less foolish than superstitious: namely those who wish to have no commerce with demons, and nevertheless use, in vain operations, things assigned to demons and therefore wholly unlawful. For they think that great and hidden power resides in characters, and for that reason they commit various errors against the faith of Christ. But since this is not the time to recount their madness, let us pursue our subject.

Why good and just men do not obtain command over demons must be briefly learned. Just as likeness of wills makes wicked and impious men equal to demons, so unlikeness of wills makes the good and just entirely opposed to them. But among opposites and things unlike there can be no familiarity; rather, continual resistance and hatred prevail. Where there is no familiarity contracted by likeness of wills, there can be neither confidence of one toward the other, nor mutual cooperation in a marvelous operation. Nor do you, glorious Caesar, a man, the great ruler and prince of men, admit as your familiar anyone wholly contrary and unlike to you in morals and constantly resisting your will.

Good and upright men, because they always resist the most depraved will of demons, can in no way pass into their fellowship, for they neither wish nor consent to be their familiars, but flee and detest their encounter with all their strength. Therefore they do not obtain over them that fictitious command of which we have spoken. For no familiarity is secure where no likeness of wills has preceded it; nor can there be concord among opposites, nor friendship where the will is unlike.

Yet demons do not obey all the wicked and reprobate indiscriminately, but only those with whom they are allied by pacts and services, and whom they cannot otherwise have faithful to them; when invoked, they willingly come, though they falsely claim that they are compelled. Therefore it is not to be wondered at, most excellent Caesar, that malignant spirits sometimes seem to obey depraved and perverse men, whom, as we say, malice has made like them and destruction against the human race has made harmonious with them.

But far be it from every Christian to wish to command demons by a depraved likeness of will, since if anyone begins in this life to have fellowship with malignant spirits, in the future he will burn with them without end.

But why can good and just men not command the holy angels of God, into whose likeness of good will they have passed? I think that, from what has already been said, the solution to this question would easily be given, if the difference of understandings is recalled to mind. For although there are many men established in the Church of God whose righteousness benefits many unto salvation, nevertheless in our times very few of the common sort advance so far that, by the merit of holiness, they are either feared by demons or received by angels into the fellowship of familiarity. Hence it happens that men of our age neither command malignant spirits by merit of holiness, nor deserve to be familiar with the holy angels. But if any have advanced to that degree of holiness by which, performing miracles in the Church, the saints once advanced, then they are already able powerfully both to command demons and to have familiar fellowship with the blessed spirits.

For it is certain that holy men beloved by God in the primitive Church of Christians once bestowed greater benefits upon mortals by the cooperation of good spirits than the impiety of depraved men could ever have inflicted harms by the ministry of demons. For whoever has become a true worshiper of God, like the holy angels, can do many wondrous things by prayers.

On the Power of Witches.

QUESTION SIX.

The sixth question of your unconquered Majesty was: Whence comes this power so great in acts of witchcraft, by which they can accomplish so many various and wondrous things, even in one hour such and so great things as none of the good could do in his whole life? To this question, if we wish to answer briefly, we must necessarily say that all power is from the Lord God, without whom no creature can do anything.

26
QUAESTIO SEXTA. atura. Dicit enim in sancto Euangelio Christi: Sine me nihil potestis facere. Unde manifestum est, quod omnis potestas faciendi aliquid hominibus a domino deo, & non aliunde conceditur, siue bonum homines siue malum operentur. Hinc sanctissimus Praef. Augustinus dicit: Voluntas dei est prima et summa causa omnium corporalium spe cierum ac motionum, nihilque fit in ista tota? creaturae amplissima et immensa republica viibiliter, quod non de interiori, invisibili atque intelligibili aula summi Imperatoris aut iubeatur aut permittatur, secundum ineffabilem iustitiam praemiorum atque poenarum. Unde non est dubitandum Caesar, quod potestas illa maleficarum in qua mirandos (cooperatione daemonum) horren dosque producunt effectus, a domino deo cõcedat cuius voluntati nemo potest resistere et fine cuius influxu nec manum homo po test mouere. Concludunt enim sancti doctores, quod neque daemones neque malefice quicquam facere possunt, siue hominem laedere siue iumentum, nisi omnipotens deus velit, consentiat, potestatae concedat, ut faciât quid pueris a voluntate decreverit. Nisi de us cõsentiat et velit, nihil potestois creatura, alio IOH. TRIT. ABB. SPAN. aliquin si fieri aliquid eo no volente et consentente posset, sequeretur necessario deum esse infirmum, qui prohibere non posset, qd fieri inuitus permittere cogeretur. Sed quoniam omnis homo inquantum creatura est à deo dependet, nihil posset agere sine illius voluntate, à quo et velle habet et posse. Quicquid igitur maleficae faciunt, deo fit permissente, sine cuius voluntate nihil possunt: qua vt possint quod volunt, nifi deus concesserit neqy à se neqy à daemoibus coleuerent. Ois itac postestas a dho deo est, in quo et funt omnia et mouentur, sicut in prima rerum omnium causa: quoniam à quo libertatem arbitrii accepimus, ab ipso etià posse quod vossumus habemus. Sed cum maleficarum fit multum confusus intellectus, non arte huae mana perpestrant mala quae faciunt, sed co operatione daemonum quos vt natura subtiles, ita et experientia longa fecit ad producendum mirada velociae. Non enim causans cur mirandi effectus maleficarum ab huilus modi medis, quibus vtuntur ad maleficandum, vt sunt capita moctuorũ, bufones, fers pêtes, characteres, imagines et his similias sed ab instituete haec signa diabolo, q cu sit super bissimus, deo cupit in oibus videri cõparandus. QUAESTIO SEXTA. dus. Enimuero quemadmodum omnipotens deus qaedam in ecclesia sua sacramenta instituit, quae dignè ministrantibus ipso assistente salutarem designant et producunt effectum, ipso qui instituit operante salutet: ita et diabolus qui nihil plus appetit quam aestimari deo aequalis, quaedam signa tangit sacramenta instituit, quibus inuocatus ab his quibus confederatus pactis opator malignus assistit, & quoties deus permiserit, quod rogatur malum efficit: si non permiserit, ille nihil omnino facit. Omnium liquidem effeta omnium necromanticorum et malificarum operator diabolus est: p applicationem mediorum, quae prius ipse instituit, in materia subiectam, opus producit optatum, aliquando realiter, aliquando solum apparenter. Mulieres autem malefice, quae iam voluntate de prauata et consenfu in consortium daemonum per pacta transierunt, notas quaedam et signa symbolica ab ipfis recipiunt, quibus aduocati mox daemones occurruunt. Nihil in his pernitiiosis operationibus daemonum fortius itulca credulitate maleficularum, quae pactis augetur et votis: quoniam quaeto vel daemonibus vel eorum signis firmiorem ad hibuerint fidem, taeco velociorem assequuntur

QUESTION SIX.

For he says in the holy Gospel of Christ: “Without me you can do nothing.” Hence it is clear that every power of doing anything is granted to human beings by the Lord God, and from nowhere else, whether people do good or evil. Thus the most holy Father Augustine says: “The will of God is the first and highest cause of all bodily forms and motions; and nothing happens visibly in this whole vast and immense commonwealth of creation unless it is either commanded or permitted from the inner, invisible, and intelligible court of the supreme Emperor, according to the ineffable justice of rewards and punishments.”

Therefore, Caesar, it must not be doubted that that power of witches by which, through the cooperation of demons, they produce wondrous and dreadful effects is granted by the Lord God, whose will no one can resist and without whose influence a person cannot even move his hand. For the holy doctors conclude that neither demons nor witches can do anything, whether harming a human being or an animal, unless almighty God wills it, consents to it, and grants the power, so that they may do what he has decreed by his will [unclear]. Unless God consents and wills, no creature has any power; otherwise, if something could be done when he did not will or consent, it would necessarily follow that God was weak, since he could not prevent what he would be forced unwillingly to permit. But since every human being, insofar as he is a creature, depends on God, he can do nothing without the will of him from whom he has both the will and the power.

Whatever witches do, therefore, is done by God’s permission; without his will they can do nothing. And unless God had granted that they could do what they wish, they could obtain it neither from themselves nor from demons. Thus all power is from the Lord God, in whom all things exist and are moved, as in the first cause of all things; for from him from whom we have received freedom of choice, from him also we have the power to do what we can.

But since the understanding of witches is very confused, they do not perpetrate the evils they do by human art, but by the cooperation of demons, whom nature has made subtle and long experience has made swift in producing marvels. For the causes of the wondrous effects of witches are not such means as they use for witchcraft, such as owls’ heads, toads, serpents, characters, images, and things like these, but the devil who instituted these signs; for since he is most proud, he desires in all things to be seen as comparable to God.

Indeed, just as almighty God instituted certain sacraments in his Church, which, when worthily administered, signify and produce a saving effect through his own assistance, he who instituted them working salvation, so also the devil, who desires nothing more than to be considered equal to God, instituted certain signs as sacraments. When he is invoked by these by those with whom he has been joined in covenants, the malignant worker assists them, and as often as God permits, he brings about the evil that is requested; if God does not permit it, he does absolutely nothing.

For the devil is the worker of all the effects of all necromancers and witches: by applying the means which he himself first instituted to the subject matter, he produces the desired work, sometimes in reality, sometimes only in appearance. But witch-women, who have now passed over with depraved will and consent into the fellowship of demons through pacts, receive from them certain marks and symbolic signs, by which the demons, once summoned, immediately appear. In these destructive operations of demons nothing is stronger than the foolish credulity of little witches, which is increased by pacts and vows; for the firmer the faith they have placed either in demons or in their signs, the more swiftly they obtain [unclear].
