Visque adeo quippe diabolus elatus superbia ecclesiam CHRI STI aemulatur, vt quemadmodum non ordinatus Christi corpus non potest confis cere, quantumlibet verba consecrationis proferat: sic etiam daemon ţutuis inuocan ti et signa fiue characteres ostêdêti, quem pa to si bi non nouit subieçtum, aut nunç aut garo concurrit. Nam si omnibus fe inuo cantibus sine pactis passim interpositis oc curreret, non tot maleficas sibi proprietatis jure dicatas possideret. Hinc est, quod mul ti prophanis artibus dediti, daemones ad cir culum, ad speculum, fiue ad quaelibet alia re ceptacula horrendis coniurationibus con uocare laborantes, nullum consequuntur effectum: quoniam aut dei obstatimperî um, aut diabolus contemnit curiosum hos minem si bi homagio non dicatum: Tria ere nim requirûtur ad maleficium, sine quibus F 2 nullũ IOH. TRITTEN. ABB. SPAN. nullum constat esse perpetratum. Animo furor ac depravata voluntate malefica, cooperatio quoque familiaris diabolica, & ante omnia permisso divino. Quod si vnum istorum non concurret, maleficium perpetra-ri non poterit. Nam si Deus non permetteret nec diabolus quicquam nec malefica posset. Et si diabolus pravae mulieris voluntati non occurreret, nullum illa maleficium perpetra-ret. Rursum si malefica defuerit, diabolus maleficium nullatenus consummabit. Vtitur enim voluntate furentis maleficae diabolus tanquam artifex instrumento ad operandũ fine qua non posset inferre maleficium. Et sicuti daemones in potestate acumineque subtilitatis ab inuicem differunt: ita maleficae potestas non est in omnibus una, sed in singulis prout daemonibus concurrunt natura subtilioribus, vel grossioribus, diversa. Muls ta enim sunt genera daemonum, & certis inter se gradibus distant, ratione locorum in quae cadentes à principio sunt detrusi. Pris mum quidem genus daemonum appellatur igneum, quod circa superiorem peruagatur aerem, nec vnquam ante iudicij diem ad inferiora demergetur: sed continue sub regionibus permanetës lunaribus nullum habet cum

with these cooperating in the operation. For the exceedingly savage corruption of the witches’ will in a certain way turns them into frenzy; when this has seized their mind, demons at once attach themselves to the raging women, and, summoned by pacts and signs, by God’s permission accomplish for the madwomen the effect of destruction.

Plato relates something similar in his book on poetic frenzy, saying: just as Bacchic women, when their mind is not sound, draw honey and milk from rivers, but when their mind is sound cannot draw them. This is brought about by their spirit, carried outside itself into fellowship with an evil demon. We know by experience that witches have drawn butter from rushing rivers at certain times, which cannot in any way happen otherwise than by the ministry of a demon.

In like manner, when they have been led into hatred of some man or beast, sighing for its destruction, they are driven by a most grievous frenzy, thinking of nothing in their mind except revenge. They take things known and familiar to them for witchcraft, invoke demons, show the signs appointed by them, and also the characters; and what they cannot accomplish by their own power, they obtain by the demons’ ministry.

But another person, who is not subject to the demons by pact and surrender, even if he knows the things suited to witchcraft and also the manner of operating, and although he displays the signs, nevertheless rarely obtains the effect, because he is not counted among the demons’ familiars. For the devil, swollen with pride, imitates the Church of Christ to such a degree that, just as an unordained man cannot consecrate the body of Christ, however much he may utter the words of consecration, so also a demon either never or rarely comes to the aid of one who invokes him and shows signs or characters, if he does not know that person to be subject to him by pact.

For if he came indiscriminately to all who invoked him without pacts having been made, he would not possess so many witches dedicated to him by right of ownership. Hence many who are given over to profane arts, striving by dreadful conjurations to call demons to a circle, a mirror, or any other receptacles, obtain no effect, because either God’s command stands in the way, or the devil despises the curious man who has not been dedicated to him by homage.

For three things are required for witchcraft, without which it is agreed that none is perpetrated: fury in the mind and a depraved will in the witch, the cooperation of a familiar demon, and before all else divine permission. If one of these does not concur, witchcraft cannot be perpetrated. For if God did not permit it, neither the devil nor the witch could do anything. And if the devil did not meet the will of the wicked woman, she would perpetrate no witchcraft. Again, if the witch is lacking, the devil will by no means bring the witchcraft to completion.

For the devil uses the will of the raging witch as an artisan uses an instrument for working; without it he could not inflict witchcraft. And just as demons differ from one another in power and keenness of subtlety, so the power of a witch is not one and the same in all, but differs in each according as demons of a subtler or grosser nature concur with them. For there are many kinds of demons, and they stand apart from one another by fixed degrees, according to the places into which they were cast down when they fell in the beginning.

The first kind of demons is called fiery; it ranges about the upper air and will never be plunged down to the lower regions before the day of judgment, but, remaining continually beneath the lunar regions, has no [unclear].

28
QVAESTIO SEXTA. cum hominibus in terra commertiũ. Quod vero sub luna permaneant, sanctus testatur Augustinus in opere de agone Christiano, sic dicenst Daemones non habitant in coelo ubi sol et stellae sunt, sed omnes sub regione lunari versantur. Hinc motus, vt reor Apus leius daemonia dixit animalia esse ignita et propterea quod Aristoteles confirmavit in fornacibus ardentibus quaedam animalia parua saepius visa volitasse pennulis apta, q totum aeuum suum diversantur in igne, quo niam cum igne oriuntur et cum eo extinguent, & ad suum unde venerant locum, eua nescientes redeunt. Nulla sunt eis cum males fics consortia, quoniam cum demorentur in igne propter subtilitatem suam, non pos sunt corpus induere grossum hue aereum. Secundum genus aereum dicitur: quod in aere oberrans nobis propinquae commoratur. Siquidem posunt ad inferiora descender, & assumptis de crassiore aere corpori b qndoque visibles hominibus apparere. Aera pmittete deo saepius turbant, tonitrua et tempestates concitant, & omnes simul in perniciem humani generis conspirant. Ma re hominum affectionibus mouentur passi onum, superbia maxime et invidia, tangun F 3 turq IOH. TRITTEN. ABB. SPAN. turque pertubationib. continuis, & nec soli do vestiuntur corpore, nec vno consistunt loco. Neque vnam omnes formam habent, sed plurimas, easque saepius mutant secundum varietatem affectionum, quibus vel occurrunt maleficarum carminibus evocati, vel impulsi perturbatione ad noscendum. Habent enim omnino violentum et furiosum morem turbationibus plenum. Vnde vehementer malefacti et per turbati repentinas plurimum machinantes tur infidiast et dum suas agunt incursiones, partim latere volunt, partim inferunt violentiam. Maleficae horum daemonum co operatione suffultae, tanto sunt ad maleficandum potentiores, quanto superiorem ex eorum ordine concurrentem fuerint affecutae. In vita sancti A N T O N I I diuus Athanafius aerem plenum dixit esse dae monibus quod et Mercurius ante dixerat er maximus, nullam videlicet mundi parte daemonum praesentia destitutam. Sanctus quoque praeful AMBROSIVS dicit: Pienus est mundus sanctarum virtutum, quia plenus est nequitiarum. Vnde Platonici daemones in aere volantes in mo dum QUAESTIO SEXTA. dum densissimae niuis ignitae cupientibus tradidere visibles, si aliquamdiu versus coelum sole splendente irreuerberatis oculis continuauerint obtutus: Sed nescio an in aere causetur obiectum ex consistentia reali, vel certe oculorum motus interclusus repreaesentet imagines fallat: non sine detrimento sensus, tamen leui, praemissorum cepi experimentum. Tertium vero genus daemonum terrestrium dicitur, quos prolapso e coelo in terram pro luis demeritis minime dubitamus. De his sanctissimus praesul et martyr CHRISTI Theophorus quondam Ignatius in epistola quadam ita scripsit ad Ephefios: Nihil melius est, quam pacem habere, in qua omne telum evacuatur aereorum simul et terrestrium spirituum. Ex his autem daemonibus alij versantur in syluis atque nemoribus, qui venatoribus ponunt insidias: alij vero patulis degunt in campis, qui nocte aberrare faciunt itinerantes: non nulli commorantur in locis abditis atque F 4 cauer IOH. TRITTEN. ABB. SPAN. cauernistreliqui caeteris minus furiosi et per turbati demorari cum hominibus in obscu ro delectantur. Nō vno ducūt affectu, sed va riosq̄m alis sunt alijs minus deprauati:quan quam omnes sint malis turbationibus ple ni. Ex his quidam solis gaudent illusioni bus territare homines, alis praedictionibus futurorum in admirationem sui trahere cu piunt audientes. Nonnulli vero ad hoc sum mo conatu laborant, vt homines irrationa bili furore turbatos aut melancholia furens tes terreant, laedant, vel occidant:quod expe rientia saepeus factum agnouimus. Hinc san ctus IOHANNES CHRYSSOTOMVS in tertio libro de prouidentia ad Stagirium monachum dicit: Omni actione diaboli ca potentior est ad non nocendum moer ris magnitudor: quia daemon quoscunque sue perat per moerorem superat. Eum si auferas nihil à daemone quisquam laedi poterit. Hoc autem daemonum genus raro est maleficis famikare propter inconstantiam affectio num et leuitatem, qua territare multos ga dent potius, quam vnius mulierculae subefte imperio. Commorantur tamen interdum, vt pallicentur vesanis, in vitro vel in crys tallo

That they remain beneath the moon, however, Saint Augustine bears witness in his work On the Christian Struggle, saying thus: “Demons do not dwell in heaven, where the sun and the stars are, but all move about beneath the lunar region.” Moved by this, as I think, Apuleius said that demons are fiery animals; and for this reason Aristotle confirmed that in burning furnaces certain small animals have often been seen flying about, fitted with little wings, which spend their whole lifetime in fire, since they arise with the fire and are extinguished with it, and return, unknowing, to the place from which they had come. They have no fellowship with witches, since, dwelling in fire because of their subtlety, they cannot put on a gross body, nor even an aerial one.

The second kind is called aerial: it wanders in the air and dwells near us. Indeed, they can descend to lower places, and, taking bodies from the thicker air, sometimes appear visibly to human beings. When God permits, they often disturb the air, raise thunder and storms, and all conspire together for the destruction of the human race. They are moved by men’s greater passions, especially pride and envy; they are touched by continual disturbances, are not clothed with a solid body, and do not remain in one place. Nor do they all have one form, but many, and they change these quite often according to the variety of their affections, either when they come, summoned by the spells of witches, or when they are driven by disturbance to do harm. For they have an altogether violent and furious disposition, full of disturbances. Hence, being exceedingly wicked and disordered, they contrive many sudden ambushes; and while they make their assaults, some wish to lie hidden, others inflict violence. Witches, supported by the cooperation of these demons, are the more powerful for doing witchcraft, the higher in their order the demon they have obtained as an accomplice.

In the life of Saint Antony, the divine Athanasius said that the air is full of demons; and Hermes Trismegistus had said the same before him, namely that no part of the world is bereft of the presence of demons. The holy bishop Ambrose also says: “The world is full of holy powers, because it is full of wickednesses.” Hence the Platonists have related that demons flying in the air like very thick fiery snow become visible to those who desire it, if for some time, while the sun is shining, they keep their gaze fixed toward heaven with unblinking eyes. But I do not know whether the object in the air is caused by a real substance, or whether the checked motion of the eyes represents deceptive images; nevertheless, though not without some injury to the sense, yet a slight one, I have made trial of the things just mentioned.

The third kind is called that of terrestrial demons, whom we do not in the least doubt to have fallen from heaven to earth for their own deserts. Concerning these, that most holy bishop and martyr of Christ, Theophorus, once Ignatius, wrote thus in a certain letter to the Ephesians: “Nothing is better than to have peace, in which every weapon of the aerial and terrestrial spirits alike is made void.” Of these demons, some dwell in woods and groves, laying snares for hunters; others live in open fields, making travelers wander off course at night; some dwell in hidden places and caverns; the rest, less furious and disturbed than the others, delight in dwelling obscurely with human beings. They are not led by one affection, but by various ones, and some are less depraved than others, although all are full of evil disturbances. Some of these rejoice in frightening human beings with mere illusions; others desire to draw their hearers into admiration of themselves by predictions of future events. Some, however, strive with the greatest effort to terrify, injure, or kill human beings troubled by irrational frenzy or raging with melancholy; and we have learned by experience that this has often happened. Hence Saint John Chrysostom, in the third book On Providence to the monk Stagirius, says: “The greatness of grief is more powerful than every action of the devil in preventing harm; for whatever men a demon overcomes, he overcomes through grief. If you take that away, no one will be able to be harmed by a demon.” This kind of demon, however, is rarely familiar to witches, because of the inconstancy of their affections and the lightness by which they delight more in terrifying many people than in being subject to the command of one little woman. Yet sometimes, to flatter the insane, they dwell in glass or in crystal.

29
QUAESTIO SEXTA. Atto siue in speculo, & carminibus concitati responsa dant mulieribus, & si quis venturus eis maledixisset in via, praenunciant. Et hoc maleficarum genus multum aliquoties differt à reliquis: quoniam quod ille maleficio reddunt infirmum, istae curare pollicent. Verum quia maleficium vt plurimum repellunt maleficio, earae accessus interdicitur ab ecclesia omni Christiano. Quartum genus daemonum nuncupatur aquaticum, quoniam se humoribus immergens, circa lacus et fluvios habitat, ira plenum, turbatam, inquietum et fraudulentum, quod in mari tempestates concitat, nauigiacy demergens in profundum, multis vita auffert in aquis. Et isti demones quoties assumunt corpus visibile, in lexu freñntius apparet foemineo, & in masculino rarius videt, ppteraea q̄ in locis ȳsan tur humidis, & mollioraem vitae ductum sequuntur, nec vile schema facile caeterorum consuetudine possunt assumere. Vnde Naia das Nereidas et aquarum nymphas, n̄ masculino sexu, sed foeminino dudum nomina uit antiquitas. A nostris autae aquaticae mulieres, id est, wasser frauwen, communi vocae bulo dicuntur. Qui vero habitant in locis fícioribus et subaridis, quoties hoibus corpo F 5 raliter JOHAN. TRIT. ABBA. SPAN. raliter apparent visibles, in viros se transformant. Diuersa q̄ species assumunt bestiarum, prout varijs tanguntur affectio nibus. Sancti aut angeli, quoniam affectio neq̄ variantur, uniformiter semper appa rent in forma virili. Nusq̄ em legimus scriptum, q̄ bonus spiritet in forma sit visus muliebri, aut bestiae cuiuscq̄, sed semper in spe cie virili. At vero sapieus visi sunt daemones circa flumina et fontes in specie mulierum, aliquando chorizantes, aliquando capillos more foeminarq̄ explicantes, nonnunq̄ vero cum hominibus loquentes, & varias ludificationes exercentes. Et hoc genus daemoni non consuevit cum maleficiis habere cõmer tium, Quintum genus subterranei dicitur, quod in speluncis et cavernis montiumq̄ re motis concavitatibus demorat. Et ihi daemo nes affectione sunt pessimi, eosq̄ inuadunt maxime qui puteos et metalla fodiunt, & q̄ thesauros in terra latentes quaerunt, in per nitiem humani generis paratissimi. Hiatus efficiunt terrae, ventosq̄ flammiuomos fu scitant, & fundamenta edificiorq̄ concutiũt. Noctibus aliquado de montibus turmatim egressi, mirandas stupendasq̄ in campis du cunt choreas, & quasi vnius ducis metuẽtes imperium QVAESTIO SEXTA. imperium subito evanescunt ad signum, & ad sua diverticula reuertitur. Interdum nostrorum inter eos auditur sonitus, & se non nunquam spiritus esse hominum vita defunctorum mentiuntur. Nihil magis quaerunt quàm metum hominum et admirationem. Vnde habemus compertum, quod simpliciores hominum quosdam nonnunquam in sua latibula montium duxerunt, stupenda mirantibus ostendentes spectacula: & quos beatorum ibi sint mansiones, amicos se visuorum mentiuntur. Ex his quoque demonibus, quidam incubones sunt thesauros, quos avaritia mortalium abscondit in terram, & ne rursus in vius perveniant hominum, eos subducit, furantur, & custodunt, & quandoq de loco in locum transponunt. Ethoc genus daemonum cum maleficiis mulieribus nullum consuevit habere commertium. Sextum vero daemonum genus appellatur lucifugũ, propterea quod lucem maxime horrent et detestantur: quia nec diebus vnquam apparent, nec alio modo corpus quàm de nocte posunt assumere. Hoc est negotium quod in tenebris perambulat, genus daemonum imperfcrutabile, ac penitus tenebrosum, passionibusq frigidis agitã IOHAN. TRIT. ABBA. SPAN. agitatum, malitiosum, inquietum, & perturbatum, quod occurrentes homines nocturnis violenter comprimit horis, sapiusque deo permittente, aut flatu quosdam interficit, aut contactu. Maleficis nō conuenit hoc genus daemoni, nec carminibus artari potest, quia et lucem fugit et voces hominum, simul omnem tumultum aereum maxime ad maleficia feminarum consuevit occurre re, quoniam caeteris est omnibus magis subtile, & audacissimae temeritatis. Terrestrium quoq nonnulli maleficiis, vt est dictum, sub ieruiunt, qui tam inferiori gradu habiti maiora illa maleficia inducere minime posse. Cōstat igitur manifeste, qu tota potestas maleficarum, in qua tam miranda faciunt, daemonibus à domino deo limitata concedit, & quando ille non permitcit, nihil operant De permissione divina. Quaestio Septima. S EPrima quaestio serenissimae Maiestatis tuae ista fuit: Quare omnipotēs deus, cum sit iustus et vindex malorum, tanta maleficia

In a bowl, or in a mirror, and when stirred up by incantations, they give answers to women; and if someone who is about to come has cursed them on the road, they foretell it. This kind of witch sometimes differs greatly from the rest: for what the others make diseased by witchcraft, these promise to cure. But because they very often repel witchcraft by witchcraft, access to them is forbidden by the Church to every Christian.

The fourth kind of demons is called aquatic, because, plunging itself into watery places, it dwells around lakes and rivers. It is full of anger, troubled, restless, and deceitful; it raises storms at sea, sinks ships into the deep, and takes life from many in the waters. Whenever these demons assume a visible body, they appear more often in the female sex, and are more rarely seen in the male, because they remain in damp places and follow a softer manner of life, and cannot easily assume a male form in the manner of the others. Hence antiquity long ago named Naiads, Nereids, and nymphs of the waters not in the male sex but in the female. Among our people they are commonly called aquatic women, that is, wasser frauwen. But those who dwell in drier and somewhat arid places, whenever they appear bodily and visibly to human beings, transform themselves into men.

They also assume different forms of beasts, according as they are touched by various affections. But the holy angels, because they are not varied by affection, always appear uniformly in male form. For nowhere do we read it written that a good spirit was seen in the form of a woman or of any beast, but always in a male form. Demons, however, have very often been seen around rivers and springs in the shape of women, sometimes dancing, sometimes spreading out their hair after the manner of women, and sometimes speaking with human beings and carrying out various mockeries. And this kind of demon is not accustomed to have dealings with acts of witchcraft.

The fifth kind is called subterranean, because it dwells in caves and caverns and in the remote hollows of mountains. These demons are the worst in disposition, and they especially attack those who dig wells and mines and those who seek treasures hidden in the earth, being most ready for the destruction of the human race. They make openings in the earth, stir up flame-breathing winds, and shake the foundations of buildings. Sometimes by night they come out from the mountains in troops, lead wonderful and astonishing dances in the fields, and, as though fearing the command of one leader, suddenly vanish at a signal and return to their hiding places. At times the sound of our people is heard among them, and sometimes they falsely claim that they are the spirits of human beings who have departed this life. They seek nothing more than the fear and amazement of human beings.

Hence we have ascertained that they have sometimes led some of the simpler sort of men into their hiding places in the mountains, showing astonishing sights to those who marveled, and falsely claiming that the dwellings of the blessed are there and that they are friends of those who see them. Some of these demons also brood over the treasures which the greed of mortals has hidden in the earth; and lest they come again into human use, they carry them off, steal them, guard them, and sometimes transfer them from place to place. This kind of demon is not accustomed to have any dealings with women’s witchcraft.

The sixth kind of demons is called light-fleeing, because they especially dread and detest the light: for they never appear by day, nor can they assume a body in any other way than by night. This is the business that walks about in darkness, an inscrutable and utterly dark kind of demons, driven by cold passions, malicious, restless, and disturbed. It violently oppresses people who meet it in the hours of night, and more often, when God permits, kills some either by its breath or by its touch. This kind of demon does not associate with witches, nor can it be constrained by incantations, because it flees both light and the voices of human beings, and likewise every disturbance of the air.

The aerial kind is especially accustomed to come to the witchcraft of women, because it is subtler than all the rest and of the boldest rashness. Some of the terrestrial demons also, as has been said, serve acts of witchcraft; but since they are held to be of a lower rank, they cannot bring about those greater acts of witchcraft. It is therefore plainly established that the whole power of witches, by which they do such astonishing things, is granted to demons within limits set by the Lord God; and when he does not permit it, they accomplish nothing.

30
QUAESTIO SEPTIMA. Ieficia in pernitiem humani generis fieri per mittat quibus no folum peccatores, sed etia innocentes multi pereunt grauiter cruciat? Ad hanc quaestionem taliter me dudũ corã Maiestate tua coustitutum memini respon: disse: Omnipotẽs deus iustus et rectus, pius et misericors, quicquid permittit, iuste per: mittit, quoniam iustus est, & non est apud illum inigtast sed omnia in vero iudicio que fiunt, aut facit, aut permittit. Cum ergo que ritur, quare deus mala fieri pmittit? Respon demus: Ideo permittit, quia iustus est. Non videatur maiestati tuae o Caesar, quam dedi mus absurda respōsio: quoniam diuinae bo nitati non praejudicat vllatenus, q̄ mala fie ri iustissima ratione permittit: potius autem praejudicaret, si mala in praesentí mundo fie ti non permetteret. Enimuero si non permit teret fieri mala, iam homo peccare non pol: set, est certe impeccabilis: quod eius naturẽ non conuenit, cui ab initio liberum arbitriũ cōditor omnium dedit. Homo etenim crea: tura cum sit, & non creator, est necessario tã ad bonum convertibilis, q̄ ad malum, cuius esse dependet à summo creaturarum opifice oim, quemadmodum à causa sui esse omne causatum. Creare vero soli deo relictum est q̄ est IOHAN. TRIT. ABBA. SPAN. qui est incorruptibilis et sempiternus: corrupibile auté omne necessario deficit, conservatur autem bonitate creatoris, sdiu causae influentiam non amittit. Vnde fieri nec potuit, nec decuit, q̄ homo ex conditione sua naturae crearet impeccabilis, quo solus gaue det naturaliter opifex oim deus, qui est incõ mutabilis et sempiternus. Quoties vero con fertur homini, vt peccare non posse videat, nec libertas arbitrii tollitur, nec possibilitas simpliciter auertur, fed volũtas in bono cos firmatur. Et quotiescunque hoc donũ confer tur craturae, munus est gratiae, non naturae. Dicit enim scriptura: Deus ab initio creavit hominẽ, & reliquit eũ in manu consilii sui. Nam proprie loquẽdo esse non posteft, vt ho mo mortalis in originali displicentia conce ptus, & liberẽ habeat arbitriũ, & no possit co mittere peccatũ. Dicit enim sanctisimus Pre ful Augustinet: Prima libertas volũtatis erat posse peccare, nouissima erit in gloria mul tomagis no posse peccare. Itaç; fi homo pe care non posset, propriae voluntatis suae do minium non haberet. Vnde quamuis omni potens deus peccatum non velit, peccare ta men homines, & malum facere iuste permit tit:quatenus libertate arbitriũ permanente, & vir QUAESTIO SEPTIMA, & virtus boni operis meritum, & pravitas voluntaria recipiat quod fecerit malum. Ne mo enim aut bene facit, aut peccat inuitus. Iuste igitur omnipotens deus peccare et ma lum facere homines permittit, quibus à prin cipio libertatem arbitrii concessit. Sunt autem multae rationes à sanctis doctoribus dudum assignatae, quare omnipotens ma leficia tanta fieri per daemonum coopera tionem permitteat: quarum ordine necessa rio breuiter faciemus mentionem. Pris ma est, ve divinae manifestetur excellentia potentatis, qui solus est incommutabilis, & supra ommem longe positionem. Omnis autem creatura mutabilis ad incommuta bilem creatorem nullam habet comparas tionem. Vnde in Numeris legitur: Non est deus quasi homo, vt mentiatur, nec vt fi lius hominis vt mutetur. In I S A I A quoque dicitur: Deus fidelis absque inqui rate, iustus et rectus. In libro etiam T O: B I AE scribitur: Iustus es domine, & omnia iudicia tua vera sunt, & omnes viae tuae misericordia, veritas, & iudicium. Et in libro sancti lob legimus: Absit à deo impeitas, & ab omnipotente iniquitas. Opus

QUESTION SEVEN.

Why does he permit acts of sorcery to be done for the destruction of the human race, by which not only sinners but also many innocents perish and are grievously tormented? I remember that, when I was long ago placed before your Majesty, I answered this question in this way: Almighty God, just and upright, loving and merciful, whatever he permits, permits justly, because he is just, and there is no injustice with him; but all things that are done, he either does or permits in true judgment. Therefore, when it is asked why God permits evils to be done, let us answer: he permits them because he is just.

Let not the answer I have given seem absurd to your Majesty, O Caesar, since it in no way prejudices the divine goodness that he permits evils to be done for a most just reason; rather, it would prejudice it if he did not permit evils to be done in the present world. For indeed, if he did not permit evils to be done, then man could not sin, and would certainly be incapable of sin; but that does not belong to his nature, to whom the Creator of all things gave free will from the beginning. For since man is a creature and not the Creator, he is necessarily capable of turning both to good and to evil, since his being depends on the supreme Maker of all creatures, just as every caused thing depends on the cause of its being. But to create has been left to God alone, who is incorruptible and everlasting; every corruptible thing, however, necessarily falls away, yet is preserved by the goodness of the Creator so long as it does not lose the influence of its cause.

Therefore it neither could nor should have happened that man, according to the condition of his nature, should be created incapable of sin; for that belongs naturally only to God, the Maker of all things, who is unchangeable and everlasting. But whenever it is granted to a man that he seems unable to sin, the freedom of the will is not taken away, nor is possibility simply removed, but the will is confirmed in the good. And whenever this gift is granted to a creature, it is a gift of grace, not of nature. For Scripture says: God created man from the beginning and left him in the hand of his own counsel.

For, properly speaking, it cannot be that mortal man, conceived in original displeasure, both has free will and cannot commit sin. For the most holy bishop Augustine says: The first freedom of the will was to be able to sin; the last, in glory, will be much more to be unable to sin. And so, if man could not sin, he would not have mastery over his own will. Therefore, although almighty God does not will sin, nevertheless he justly permits men to sin and to do evil, so that, while freedom of will remains, both the virtue of a good work may receive its reward and voluntary wickedness may receive the evil it has done. For no one either does good or sins unwillingly.

Therefore almighty God justly permits men to sin and to do evil, since he granted them freedom of will from the beginning. Now many reasons have long since been assigned by the holy doctors why the Almighty permits such great acts of sorcery to be done through the cooperation of demons; of these we shall necessarily make brief mention in order.

The first is that the excellence of the divine power may be manifested, for he alone is unchangeable and far above every [unclear]. Every mutable creature has no comparison with the unchangeable Creator. Hence it is read in Numbers: God is not like a man, that he should lie, nor like a son of man, that he should change. In Isaiah also it is said: God is faithful, without iniquity, just and upright. In the book of Tobit too it is written: You are just, O Lord, and all your judgments are true, and all your ways are mercy, truth, and judgment. And in the book of holy Job we read: Far be impiety from God, and iniquity from the Almighty. The work [unclear].

31
JOHAN. TRIT. ABBA. SPAN. Opus enim hominis reddet ei, & iuxta vias singulorũ restituet eis. Omnis igitur homo qui suam ignorantiam et infirmitatem reette intelligit, q̄ sit nihil comparatus ad creas torem fuũ, patenter agnoscit. Iuste nanget de us permittit peccare hominem, quo et libera tas continuetur arbitrii, & excellentia homi nibus innotefcat magni dei. Secunda ratio est, vt imperscrutabilis dei sapientia innotefcat mortalibus, qua nouit ex nostris malis elicere bonum, cum vnius peccatum alteriet facit esse meritum ad virtutis incrementum Nam fi malum fieri non permetteret, q̄ no strum intelligeret bonum? Facit enim deus bonum et ordinat mala vero non facit, sed ab impiis facta ne inordinate veniant, ipse disponit. Neq̃ malitia hominum dei voluntatem impedit, neq̃ potest homo quicq̃, q̃ deus non permettit. Tertia vero causa est, q̃ omnipotens fieri maleficia permettit, vt ma nifestet suam clementissimam bonitatem in eos, qui peccauerunt et egerunt poenitentiã, quam nullatenus posset ostendere, si creatu ram n̄o permetteret peccare. Nam fi nullus effet peccator, nec deus posset esse miserator. Sed quoniam in multis offendimus omnes, ubiq̃ deus inuenit q̃d remittat, ubiq̃ reus occurrit QUAESTIO SEPTIMA. occurrit, in quo suam misericordiā pius con- ditor ostendat. Vnde S. Praeful Augustinus Si leuis morbus esset, contemneretur medici- cus, non quaereretur: si medicus non quaer- retur, morbus non finiretur. Ideo ubi abundau- tavit peccatum, abundauit et gratia, quae so- la discernit redemptos à perditis, quos in vnu coacervat massa pditionis ab origine ducta creationis. Est ergo misericordia domini su- per omnia opera eius. Quarta vero ratio di- uinae permissionis est, vt iustitia creatoris in cos declaretur, qui peccauerunt, & non eges- runt poenitentiam: quoniam si omnes bene facerent et nemo peccaret, nihil haberet dei iustitia quod puniret. Vt ergo iustitia locum habeat, divina permissione creatura peccat. Iustus em est dominus, qui reddet vnicuique secundum opera voluntatis suae. Quinta ra- tio est dignitas conditionis humanae, quia si deus nō permitteret peccare hominē, brutis videretur deterior, quae nulla impellēte vios lentia naturae motibus libere vtuntur. Nam et ratione bruta careant, libere th naturae motum haet, quem sequuntur: in quoru com- paratione homo videretur inferioris condi- tionis, si libere non haberet arbitrium volū- tatis. Permisit autem homini deus voluntas G tem

For a man’s work will repay him, and according to the ways of each he will restore to them. Therefore every person who rightly understands his own ignorance and weakness openly acknowledges that he is nothing in comparison with his creator. For God justly permits man to sin, both so that freedom of choice may be preserved, and so that the excellence of the great God may become known to men.

The second reason is that the inscrutable wisdom of God may become known to mortals, by which he knows how to draw good from our evils, when he makes one person’s sin become another’s merit for an increase in virtue. For if he did not permit evil to be done, who among us would understand the good? For God makes and orders the good; but evils he does not make, though, once they have been done by the impious, he disposes them so that they do not come about without order. Nor does the malice of men hinder the will of God, nor can man do anything that God does not permit.

The third cause for which the Almighty permits evil deeds to be done is that he may manifest his most merciful goodness toward those who have sinned and done penance, which he could in no way show if he did not permit the creature to sin. For if there were no sinner, neither could God be one who shows mercy. But since in many things we all offend, everywhere God finds something to forgive; everywhere the guilty man presents himself, in whom the gracious Creator may show his mercy. Hence the holy prelate Augustine says: If the disease were slight, the physician would be despised, not sought; if the physician were not sought, the disease would not be ended. Therefore where sin abounded, grace also abounded, which alone distinguishes the redeemed from the lost, whom the mass of perdition, drawn from the origin of creation, heaps together into one. Thus the mercy of the Lord is over all his works.

The fourth reason for divine permission is that the justice of the Creator may be declared upon those who have sinned and have not done penance; since if all acted well and no one sinned, God’s justice would have nothing to punish. Therefore, so that justice may have its place, the creature sins by divine permission. For the Lord is just, and he will repay each person according to the works of his will.

The fifth reason is the dignity of the human condition, because if God did not permit man to sin, he would seem worse off than brute animals, which, with no violence compelling them, freely follow the motions of nature. For although brute animals lack reason, nevertheless they freely have the motion of nature which they follow; in comparison with them man would seem to be of an inferior condition if he did not freely have free choice of the will. But God permitted man a will.

free will, over which neither kings nor princes have command. The sixth reason is praise for the merit of steadfast human virtue, when we praise a righteous poor man because, although he could have transgressed, with the help of God’s grace he remained steadfast in good will.

The seventh reason why almighty God permits demons to do such evils through witches is that those who, having despised truth, take delight in falsehood may be utterly deceived, seduced by the devil, the inventor of falsehood. For it is fitting that enchanters and witches, who disdain to follow the saving teachings of Christ, should be deceived by demons [unclear].

33
QUAESTIO SEPTIMA. fit infirmus humani generis hostis est divis na maiestati subiectus in omnibus, manife stat. Nihil enim a se ipso potest diabolus, fed omnia que facit deo permittente facit. Cau fa igitur omnium prima, propter quam os mnipotens deus fieri maleficia permittit, in stitia est: qua libertatem quam creaturae le mel a principio contulit, ordine inuiolabili custodit. Verum quia potestas creaturae om nis a suo creatore dependentis restricta est limitata, nec diabolũ oẽ qd vult, posse ma nifestum est nec hominem voluntate quans tumlibet deprauatum. Voluntas quidem est libera, sed potestas certis et necessarijs gra dibus limitata. Quoniam quidem si demo nes possent omne quod volunt, nihil tutum in humanis permaneret, sed labefactarent Iob.18, omnia. Ligatam vero potestatem demo num historia sancti I O B manifesto demonstrat exemplo: quem non amplius tentareS atan audebat, quam ei fuerat disi pensatione diuina permittum. Christum: Nam si malos, peruersos, & infideles in corpore et in rebus tantum lädere possent, coercererentur vero ab accessu et lasione honorum atque fidelium, permissionis iustum reste videretur esse iudiciũ. Nūc aũt frequentius boni et innocentes daemonum maleficiũ infirmantur, & quandoque etiam vita priuantur vt silentio iacturam rerum temporalium, quam saepe maleficiati patiũtur, transeamus. Multis venit in scrupulum cur ista permittat omnipotens, qui nihil permittit iniuste. Huius propositũ quaetionis non alias q; à priscis atque catholicis accepi doctribus,quantum potero, breuiter necessaria sper ordinem assignabo rationes. Et pri ma quidem ratio est probatio fidei Christianorum, & experientia integritatis, vt maleficiũ daemonũ flagellati dicant in passionibus carnis, quam fidem et dilectionẽ ad deũ ha beant in abscondito mentis. In prosperis esse longanimem non est difficile, sed in aduersiũcum humili patientia à saluatorẽ fideiium prestolari auxilium, non molliũ est sed fortium et vere fidelũ Christianorũ. QUESTION SEVEN

It is manifest that the weak enemy of the human race, the devil, is in all things subject to the divine majesty. For the devil can do nothing by himself, but everything he does he does with God’s permission. Therefore the first cause of all, on account of which almighty God permits sorceries to be done, is justice: by it he preserves in inviolate order the freedom that he once bestowed upon the creature from the beginning.

But because the power of every creature dependent on its Creator is restricted and limited, it is manifest that neither the devil can do everything he wishes, nor can a man, however depraved in will. The will indeed is free, but power is limited by fixed and necessary degrees. For if demons could do everything they wish, nothing among human affairs would remain safe, but they would shake everything. The story of holy Job shows by manifest example that the power of demons is bound: Satan did not dare to tempt him any further than had been permitted to him by divine dispensation. For no one in this present world, however just or strong, could resist the fury of demons, if they could always use a free power to harm according to their own choice.

Before the Lord’s Passion they used a greater freedom of power than afterward; but when Christ tasted death for us on the altar of the cross, their power was thereafter greatly diminished, as the Savior says in the Gospel: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out.” Indeed, Christ’s humility and the perseverance of the saints have greatly restrained the boldness of demons, so that they can rightly be called inciters of evils, but by no means compellers. Nor would the devil grow strong against us unless he received strength from our sins. Hence Scripture admonishes us, saying: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” And again: “Do not give place to the devil.”

Therefore, to conclude the discussion for the understanding of the question proposed, namely why God permits so many sorceries to be done, I believe the reasons have been made sufficiently clear. For although the will of demons is always wicked, nevertheless their power can never be unjust, since what they wickedly will they have from their own choice, but what they are able wickedly to do they have only from God.

And these things have been said insofar as they concern those who do evil. But why does almighty God permit demons to harm, through the agency of witches, people who have been baptized in the name of the holy Trinity and faithfully believe in his only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ? For if they could harm only the wicked, the perverse, and unbelievers in body and possessions, but were restrained from approaching and injuring the good and faithful, the judgment of this permission would rightly seem to be just. But now the good and innocent are more often weakened by the sorcery of demons, and sometimes are even deprived of life, to pass over in silence the loss of temporal possessions that those bewitched often suffer.

It comes as a scruple to many why the Almighty permits these things, since he permits nothing unjustly. For the purpose of this question proposed, I shall briefly set forth in order, as far as I can, the necessary reasons, which I have received from none other than the ancient and Catholic teachers.

The first reason is the testing of Christians’ faith and the proving of their integrity, so that those scourged by the sorcery of demons may show, in the sufferings of the flesh, what faith and love toward God they have in the hidden part of the mind. It is not difficult to be patient in prosperity, but in adversity to await with humble patience help from the Savior of the faithful belongs not to the weak, but to the strong and truly faithful Christians. In his tribulation most holy Job learned how great a constancy of faith he had toward God, which before in tranquility he had preserved without [unclear].

Hence it must also be noted that those whom the sorceries of demons or men have in any way made sick, and who, in order to recover health, approach or consult sorcerers and enchanters, whether by themselves or through others, act against the commandments of God and the Church, and have neither true faith in God nor love for him.

For they prefer the health of mortal flesh to God, and seek salvation not from Christ but from the devil and his minister. For they would rather live healthy but unhappily in the name of the devil than suffer a little here for love of Christ and afterward rejoice with him forever. But the man who does not go to sorcerers because God has forbidden it, preferring to live in observance of God’s commandments in poverty and sickness rather than against God in riches and bodily health, truly loves God and rightly keeps the integrity of the Christian faith.

Among Christians, most sacred Caesar, men corrupt in mind and reprobate concerning the faith are not to be tolerated: those who cure the bewitched by sorceries, who reveal thefts and adulteries through the ministry of demons, who foretell the future by inspecting stones or mirrors. Do not listen, I beg you, to those who, ignorant of the divine laws, think such ministers of demons useful for your rule because they know how to undo sorceries by sorcery; for that ruinous healing of bodies brings death upon souls, and makes men withdraw entirely from God their creator and cling to impious, apostate demons, with whom after death they will be damned forever.

The second reason why almighty God permits the innocent to be harmed by sorcery is the increase of merits: namely, so that their patience, tested in tribulation, may deserve a worthier crown of glory in heaven. For, as holy Augustine says, a man is unknown to himself; sometimes he fears that he cannot bear what he can bear, and yet, when temptation comes, a man is found by himself as though by a questioner, who previously lay hidden and did not know himself.

The blessed chief apostle Peter, before temptation came upon him, was hidden both from himself and from others, thinking himself firm and strong; but that temptation came, and his weakness appeared, which had been hidden. Therefore temptation is the greatest testing of man, as Sacred Scripture testifies: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the temptation of tribulation tests righteous men.” Patience is easy in prosperity, when no adversities strike with fear. But many are the tribulations of the righteous; yet from them all our Lord Jesus Christ will deliver them.

The third reason for divine permission is the preservation of humility, so that the faithful and righteous man may always fear God and never presume upon his own strength or righteousness. Hence Scripture says of the reprobate: “They are not in the labor of men, and with men they shall not be scourged. Therefore pride has held them; they are covered with iniquity; out of their wickedness their iniquity has come forth, as it were from fatness.” It belongs to the mercy of God that he sometimes permits good and righteous men to be shaken by adversities, for he knows that in prosperity they cannot be humbled. For tribulation has made many humble whom good fortune would have made proud. Finally, the fearful imagining of sorcerers makes a good man fear his God and diligently call upon his help, so that, better defended by it, he may trust himself safe against the assaults of demons. But let no proud man, presuming on his own powers, think himself safe from the sorceries of demons; for the man whom God’s protection abandons because he is swollen with pride undoubtedly lies open to the sorceries of demons.

The fourth reason is so that there may be a distinction between the good and the bad. For Scripture says of good men beloved by God, in the Acts of the Apostles: “Through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God.” And Saint...

Verum quia purgatorii tormenta sunt horrenda atque grauissima, misericors deus poenitentes et diligit, in hac vita purgare varijs modis cooeuuit, per incômoda diversae in corpore et in rebus tribulationi. Profunt enim maleficia impiorum QUAESTIO SEPTIMA. rum bonis et iustis hominibus ad medelā, ipsis autem inferentibus ad damnationem, Sexta rō est, vt homo per incursus daemonũ maleficatus, reuocetur ad poenitentiam, & proponat in corde suo necessariam vitae emendationem. Omnipotens etenim deus non subito cum peccamus, immittic vindicatam: sed ut ad praefinitum tempus nostra expectat emendationem. Si vero poenitentiā agere neglexerimus, venit ad nos videx malorum, quando nō putamus et qui nos peccatores in tranquillitate poenitendo recognolcere contemplimus, in tribulatione ferocitatem recognoscemus. Hinc sanctus prophetā in persona dei loquitur dicens: Si dereliquint filij eius legem meam, & in iudicis meis non ambulauerint, & mandata mea non custodierint, visitabo in virga iniquitates eorum. & in verberibus peccata eorumtmiam autem meam non dilispergam abeis, nec nocebo inveritatem mea. Sunt enim multi pauperes et infirmi deo placēces boni et deuoti et humiles, quos inopia et aegritutudo corporis in dei amore conservant qui fidis

Question Seven.

The holy lover of Christ, Paul, says in a certain epistle: All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution. Likewise the most wise king Solomon says in Proverbs: Whom the Lord loves he corrects, and he takes pleasure in him as a father in a son. Is it not a very glorious Christian thing, for the love of God, patiently to endure adversities, whether they are brought upon us by wicked men or by demons? For power is granted to the devil and his ministers to harm good and just people, not for their ruin, as their persecutors suppose, but rather for the greatest and sure consolation of the soul.

For truly, when a just man lives well, harms no one, offends no one, does injury to no one, loves, fears, and venerates his God with his whole heart, keeping his commandments with all care, and nevertheless is afflicted by sorceries, whether in body, or in possessions, or in both, that man is truly blessed, because when he has been tested he will receive the crown of life which God has promised to those who love him. Everyone who lives rightly in the unity of faith of the Catholic Church of Christians, and who for the love of God patiently endures the evils he receives in this world, has a sure sign that he will persevere in the grace of God and be saved.

On the contrary, concerning the wicked and the reprobate we read written thus: Why do the impious live, raised up and strengthened with riches? Their houses are secure and at peace, and the rod of God is not upon them. They spend their days in good things, and in a moment they descend to hell. For it is a manifest sign of damnation if here you live badly in sins and vices, contrary to God, and prosper in the goods of fortune, bodily strength, and health.

The fifth reason why the Almighty permits good and just people to be afflicted by the wicked and reprobate is for the complete purification of the mind. For, as Scripture says, there is no just man on earth who does good and does not sin. But since God lets no sin pass unpunished, he ordains temporal punishments for just people, through mercy, for their offenses, but eternal punishments for the impious and reprobate, through justice. Therefore, out of mercy, he commutes eternal punishment for the penitent into temporal punishment, which they must necessarily suffer either in this world or after death in purgatory. But because the torments of purgatory are dreadful and very grave, the merciful God has been accustomed to purify in this life, in various ways, the penitents whom he loves, through the hardships of diverse tribulation in body and possessions. For the sorceries of the impious profit good and just people as a remedy, but those who inflict them they profit toward damnation.

The sixth reason is that a man, harmed by the attacks of demons, may be recalled to repentance and may set in his heart the necessary amendment of life. For almighty God does not send vengeance immediately when we sin, but waits until the appointed time for our amendment. But if we neglect to do penance, the avenger of evils comes to us when we do not expect it; and he whom we have scorned to acknowledge by repentance while we sinners were in tranquility, we shall acknowledge in tribulation by his severity. Hence the holy prophet speaks in the person of God, saying: If his sons forsake my law, and do not walk in my judgments, and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges. But my mercy I will not take away from them, nor will I harm my truth.

The seventh reason why almighty God permits the demonic sorceries to prevail against good and innocent people is that he may cut off from them too unrestrained an occasion of sinning. For there are many poor and infirm people, pleasing to God, good, devout, and humble, whom poverty and sickness of body preserve in the love of God, who [unclear].

If they were rich and exalted with honors, they would quickly flow down from the purpose of holiness into the depth of vices. It is not expedient for everyone’s salvation to have honors and riches together with health; nor does a longer life always make a person better. Therefore almighty God, wishing to show his mercy in those whom he has chosen, permits good, just, and innocent people to be subject to various calamities. And sometimes through demons, sometimes through wicked people, and sometimes by various other ways and means, he turns away riches and honors from such people, which he foreknew they would use badly, so that they may preserve humility in poverty and abasement, which, if placed in wealth and high rank, they would by no means have kept. He also very often permits them to fall into many and great illnesses, because glad health of the flesh would have brought the greatest sickness upon the mind. Finally, he permits some to be driven to death by witchcraft, so that the freedom to sin may be cut off from them, which, had they been allowed to live longer, they would have abused. Hence Scripture says of the just man: “He was taken away, lest malice should change his understanding, and lest deceit should beguile his soul.” The eighth reason for divine permission is that people may venerate the sacraments of the Church, which have great power against all the witchcrafts of malignant spirits. For one who venerates the sacraments and rites of the Catholic Church with due honor is rarely harmed by the witchcrafts of demons. And by the very confession of witches we have often heard that the hearing of Masses and the use of things blessed by the Church greatly weaken the powers of demons. For things are not blessed in the Church of God in vain, but so that they may be defenses of divine protection and may show demons signs to be feared. But concerning boys and infants who, reborn in Christ, are in some way killed by the witchcrafts of demons or of human beings, we do not doubt that divine prudence permits this to happen for their salvation, since it knows how to order all things for the better for mortals. Yet it often happens that infants perish through witchcraft because of the sins of their parents.

On the Providence of God.

Question Eight.

This was the eighth question of your Serenity: whether it can be proved by natural reason, as also by the holy Scriptures, that God has care for human affairs and actions, and a certain and infallible providence over all and each of the things that he does in the world. I remember answering this question as follows. The whole world, heaven and earth, and all things that are in them, are subject to divine providence, by whose will and command they were brought into being from the beginning. For there is nothing in the whole universe that is not governed by the providence of the Creator. Let us prove this opinion briefly, first by the Scriptures and then, as far as is permitted, by reasons. In the book of Judith we read: “All your ways are peaceful, and you have placed all judgments in your providence.” And in Ecclesiastes the most wise king Solomon speaks thus: “Do not give your mouth to make your soul sin, nor say before the angel, ‘There is no providence,’ lest the Lord, angered against your words, destroy all the works of your hands.” The clearest testimonies of providence are confirmed in the holy Gospel, when our Savior says to his disciples: “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them falls upon the earth before God.” This is a great commendation of divine providence: it has care not only for human beings, but also for tiny birds. Indeed, if the Almighty cares for such small things, who would deny that he has care for great things?

Vniuersum igitur quod vspiam est vel esse potest, sub vnius diuinae mentis imperio comprehenditur, cuius infallibile iu dicium nihil subterfugere potest. Nobis au tem inopinati casus accidentunt,quoniam mu tabiles fumus et quotidiie fere mutamur,nul lam futurorum habentes determinatam sci entiam: optimus vero ille factor omniā de us,cum sit omnino incōmutabilis, omnia no uit,omnia conspicit,omnia simul et semel in telligit: cuius providentia non fallitur, cuius voluntas nunquam variatur, cuius potētia nō frangitur, cuius ordinatio non violatur, cuius cōsiliũ nūg intercipit, etiā si mutari sen tētia ţdoque videatur. Ipe nā H que

Look at the birds of heaven, he says: they do not sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them. And a little later he adds, saying: If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is today and tomorrow is cast into the oven, how much more you, of little faith?

Almighty God, because he created all things and, when they did not exist, brought them into being, rules and governs the whole universe lest they slip and fall away. This could in no way happen if he did not have providence and care for all things. For if providence is taken away, the continuing order of the whole universe must necessarily be thrown into confusion.

But the Creator’s providence cares for all things, since he who feeds the birds, gives beasts their food, fills every living creature with blessing, and clothes the grass of the field, adorning violets and lilies with beautiful grace, cannot forget man, whom from the beginning he created in his own image. He cares for all things, who governs all things; and he bears providence not only for man, but also for all beasts, in whose dominion all things are placed, and there is no one who can resist his will in anything.

Let us therefore now consider this vast structure of the whole universe, how in its original disposition and motion it always persists in most perfect order; and, unless we shamefully depart from reason, we shall understand by the clearest reasoning that that divine and unchangeable providence preserves, directs, and governs it. Then let us contemplate all things of the earth, how most orderly each and every thing is born and proceeds in its natural disposition. This cannot happen by chance; rather, they must be moved by the will of him by whose power they were made and created.

Next, let us contemplate the earth, placed in the middle of the world as its point or center, which unfolds the circle of the whole universe at an equal distance, than which nothing more beautiful, nothing more adorned, nothing finally more delightful could offer itself to the senses for contemplation. In this point of an immense mass, enclosed by that very mass, we see all things wonderfully ordered, and nothing can be left unordered; so that all things which sometimes seem to us in some way to drift, we may know for certain do not lack their own order within the order of the universe. For by the simple and wholly unchangeable nod of God, the whole structure of the entire universe, gathered from so many diverse moving things, works together and is ruled in the most orderly way.

Certainly we see in those things that present themselves to our senses that the greater the intelligence and power that arise over time in any governor, the less can anything disordered happen there by fortuitous chance. Therefore, since that highest intellect, the creator, preserver, and ruler of all things, almighty God, rules and governs the world by his unchangeable providence, holding all things under his command, surely no place is ever left for rash chance, which would obstruct the will of so great a majesty.

Thus the whole universe, whatever exists anywhere or can exist, is contained under the command of the one divine mind, whose infallible judgment nothing can escape. But unexpected events befall us because we are changeable and are almost daily changed, having no determined knowledge of future things. Yet that best maker of all things, God, since he is wholly unchangeable, knows all things, beholds all things, understands all things together and at once. His providence is not deceived, his will is never varied, his power is not broken, his ordering is not violated, his counsel is never intercepted, even if at times his decision seems to be changed.

Therefore, if we diligently attend to these things, we shall plainly understand, as the ends of things and of motions will declare, that these lower things are made, preserved, disposed, and moved by divine providence, to whose command absolutely nothing is foreign.

Alij vero deum incorru ptibilia duntaxat curare putabant, vt sunt coelestia et substantia separata, simul et spe cies

God, the maker of the universe, both understands all things and, distinguished in a singular manner, is not divided into many things, but remains in himself one indivisible being; by beholding him as the pattern of the whole universe and the cause of cause through causes, he contemplates the cause of all things, and by contemplating all things he cares for them and provides for them, directing each one to a good end by an everlasting order. Come now, most wise Caesar: in order that we may understand the divine providence that governs all things, let us use arguments, as briefly as we can, for our purpose.

Thus, if God’s action is his own proper intelligence, as no wise man fails to admit, since it is at once most eminent and most inward, then insofar as he acts, so far he surely understands, and conversely. But he acts in individual things, not only in great things but also in the very smallest; therefore he understands individual things. For the influence of the first being extends most widely through each thing that in any way exists, following in fixed orders; and the things that act after him are moved and act everywhere by his power. Either, then, God understands or does nothing outside himself, which is false; or, by acting on all things and on each thing, he also understands them, which is true. For they would nowhere come to be unless first, to speak in our manner, they were understood by God himself, who makes them, just as they are not made by the sun and yet not perceived by it. But because the almighty understands all things and each thing that he makes, there is no doubt that he disposes, rules, and orders all things that he has made, so that things not only have from him that they exist, but also that they are certain causes of other things. And so, if things have from God that they are causes, from this they receive the proper office of a cause, that is, to preserve and care for, according to their powers, what they have made.

Therefore, if all causes have this property from the first cause, insofar as they are certain causes, then rightly does that first cause itself have this goodness and natural providence: to care for all things and each thing that it has made, inasmuch as it is supremely the cause of them all and of each one. Indeed, unless he who makes them guards them one by one, the common things that are preserved in individual things are never preserved. Nor will he preserve the whole, which consists of parts, if the parts themselves are neglected. Therefore from the intention of the first and greatest common intelligence comes the universal distinction of things; but it itself is distinguished from others by itself, and distinguishes all other things among themselves by the rule of its own knowledge. Hence, just as God knows all things and each thing most distinctly, so also he most distinctly rules, governs, and cares for them.

I think, therefore, most merciful Emperor Maximilian, that it is clear and sufficiently shown that the providence of God, the highest ruler, embraces, disposes, rules, and governs all lower things and each of them; for otherwise, without the provident disposition of one who observes them, they could in no way maintain this most beautiful order that we see. Nor am I unaware how variously the wise men of this world once held opinions about providence. Some of them thought that this world was made not by providence but by a cause; and if their opinion were true, no place would be left for providence, but all things would necessarily drift, since the world could perish by the same cause by which it was made. Against their false opinion others taught that the world could neither have been made without reason, nor certainly continue to exist unless it were ruled by the highest providence of its maker. Hence Boethius, a most Christian man, said: “O you who govern the world by everlasting reason, creator of earth and heaven, who command time to proceed from eternity, and, remaining stable, grant that all things be moved.” And again he said: “The generation of all things, the whole progress of changeable natures, and whatever is moved in any way, draw their causes, order, and forms from the stability of the divine mind.” Others, however, thought that God cares only for incorruptible things, such as the heavenly things and the separated substance, and at the same time the species [unclear].

TRIT. ABBA. SPAN. mnia produxit, sacra iterum protestate scri ptura: Tua vero pater providentia ab initio cuncta gubernat. Erubescant rigit homines mente corrupti et impii ac reprobii circa fid Christianam, qui vano loquacitate inflati p videntiam omnia scientis auferunt: & quan cum deo iniuriam faciant, non attendunt. Quid enim (vt Firmiani vtamur sententia) tam dignum tamq proprium omnipotenti deo, quam providentia? Sed si nihil prouideret, si inferiora negligent, si mortalia non curat amisit iam omnem dignitatem. Sed imposs le est sancto attestante Anselmo, deum ho norem suum perderet: qui sicut peripateticus ait, in aeternis non est malum nec corruptio nec peccatum. Qui ergo providentiam tollit, totam dei substantiam tollit: & quid dicit nisi deum non esse? Sed dicant mihi nuc qui dei providentiam negant inferiora curare. Si deus inferiora negligent, attendant quid ne cessario sequat. Si deus scienter nos negligent et contemnit, non est iam deinceps causa q ipsum vel cultu prosequamur vel religione veneremur, à quo nullum affequimur be neficium quin potius neglecti et contempti negligamus et illum iphi. Si vero nesci ens nos contemnit ac negligent, penitus iam QUAESTIO OCTAVA. iam causa non est, vt nesciētem nos et ob id nihil boni conferre potentem colamus, aut pcibus inuocemus. Nam si nō curat hũana deus, sive sciens sive nesciens, cestat ois caus fa pietatiscum fit spes nulla salutis. Quenā poteft inter mortales pietatis elle consideras tio, quae spes animarum salutis, si deus hũas na non curat? Enimuero si providentia tolli etur, quem columnus? quem adoramus? Si nō est apud deum providentia mortalium, cers te nec beneficiā praestat homibus, nec po nas defertoribus imponituneq mortales ins uare potest, nec vult, nec omnino curat, nec quid agamus aduertit, & nec preces nec os rationes cuiusquam exaudit. Cur autem illi cultum exhibemus vllum? cur honorē? cur preces? aut quare nescientem nos deum tan ropere metuimus vel timemus qui nobis ne glecis atque contemptis neque benefacere poteft neque male. Providentia eri subiata neque sanctitas negreligio subfiftet, quibus extinctis pturbatio vitae sequetur maxima, & confusio horrenda. Pietate in deum subla ga. quid iam crit respublica nifi cōfusio fem piterna? Peribit necessario fides homi num publica societasque humani generis iustitiaque ois vna fimul euanelcent et per H 4 ibunt.

But these men shamefully erred, because the Almighty has providence and care not only of all things and of incorruptible things, but also of particular and corruptible things. Hence Saint Boethius again says: “The high Creator sits upon the earth and bends the reins that govern things, king and lord, source and origin, law and wise arbiter of equity. This is [unclear] continuous love, and good things seek to be held by their end, which cannot otherwise endure unless, by love turned back again, the causes flow back to him who gave them.” But others, unable to bear that they should be neglected, exempted man from the number of corruptible things because of the pre-eminence of his intellect, saying that God has care and providence for man, but despises all the other earthly things. Against their false opinion I think enough has been said, and to bring forward many things is wholly superfluous. For Scripture says: “Men and beasts you will save, O Lord.” And in another place a certain wise man said: “The Lord made the small and the great, and he has equal care for all.” Therefore divine majesty’s providence orders, rules, disposes, and cares for all and each of the lower things, great and small, corruptible and incorruptible; its most powerful will produced all things from nothing, as sacred Scripture again bears witness: “But your providence, Father, governs all things from the beginning.”

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim.

Let men blush, then, corrupt in mind, impious, and reprobate with regard to the Christian faith, who, puffed up with empty talkativeness, take away the providence of him who knows all things, and do not consider how great an injury they do to God. For what, to use the opinion of Firmianus, is so worthy and so proper to almighty God as providence? But if he provided for nothing, if he neglected lower things, if he did not care for mortal things, he has now lost all dignity. But, as holy Anselm attests, it is impossible for God to lose his honor; he, as the Peripatetic says, in eternal things there is no evil, nor corruption, nor sin. Therefore he who removes providence removes the whole substance of God; and what does he say except that God does not exist? But now let those who deny that God’s providence cares for lower things tell me: if God neglects lower things, let them consider what necessarily follows. If God knowingly neglects and despises us, there is henceforth no reason why we should either follow him with worship or venerate him with religion, since we obtain no benefit from him; indeed, rather, being neglected and despised, let us neglect him himself also. But if he despises and neglects us unknowingly, there is now utterly no reason that we should worship one who does not know us and for that reason cannot confer any good, or invoke him with prayers. For if God does not care for human things, whether knowingly or unknowingly, every cause of piety ceases, since there is no hope of salvation. What consideration of piety can there be among mortals, what hope for the salvation of souls, if God does not care for human things? Indeed, if providence is taken away, whom do we worship? Whom do we adore? If there is with God no providence for mortals, certainly he neither grants benefits to men, nor imposes punishments on deserters; nor can he help mortals, nor does he wish to, nor does he care at all, nor does he attend to what we do, and he hears neither the prayers nor the petitions of anyone. Why, then, do we offer him any worship? Why honor? Why prayers? Or why do we fear or dread so greatly a God who does not know us, who, since we are neglected and despised by him, can do us neither good nor evil? Therefore, once providence has been removed, neither holiness nor religion will subsist; and when these have been extinguished, the greatest disturbance of life and horrible confusion will follow. With piety toward God removed, what now will the commonwealth be except everlasting confusion? Public faith among men will necessarily perish, and the society of the human race, and all justice will vanish together and perish.

IOH. TRIT. ABBA. SPAN. ibant. Quid erit de Christiana fide sentiens dum, si deus non curat humana? quid denis de salvatore omnium domino nostro le fu Christo, nisi fabula inanis et fictitium to tum reputabit, si nó est prouidētia dei morta lia curans? Proide qcquid i hac vita boni agi mus, qcquid pro dei amore mali sustinemus, vanũ é totũ ac nobis iutile, si ille de nobis cu ram non habet vllam. Videant nunc et hors reant qui prouidentiam dei negant, cum fa nem opinionis suae desperationem omnium pessimam intueantur. Nemo igitur se vani loquentia philosophorum secularium indu tus ad contemptum dei erudiat, nemo pro uidentiā summi et incommutabilis boni tol lat, nemo dignitatem creatoris omnium cor rumpat. Omnes enim qui prouidentiam ne gant diuinam, beneficis clementissimi salua toris et indignos se praestant et ingratos. Fic miter enim credendum est et nullatenus du bitandũ, hunc mūdum vniuerfum ţavisibile ţ invisibile omniag et ţngula ţ vel in coe lo sunt vel in terra et in mari, diuina proui dentia regi et gubernari, & nihil penitus in toto vniuero ab eius cura alienum. Nam et fruges et reliqua omnia quae terra parit, tem pestates quoque ac varietates tempore coeli que QUAESTIO OCTAVA. que mutationes, quibus omnia qua terra gignit, naturata pubescunt, divina providentia generi humano prestat procuratqet omnia et singula: nec solum magna sed et minima quae, vtqet adeo vt nec tenuifimum quidē arboris folium in terram decidat, sine volun tate omnipotentis dei patris, qui creavit illa et regit, & curat. Si quis autem putat hanc tantam totius vniverfi magnitudinem abvet no deo, qui solus est, non posse regi et guberna nari, nimium fallitur: & quanta sit virtus di uinae potestatis, nescire comprobatur. Enim vero qui vniverfum mundum ex nihilo po cuit in esse producere, etiam quod fecit pru dentifime in sempiternum pofet guberna re. Omnia enim nouit, omnia intelligit, om nia potest, qui solus omnipotens omnia cre auit. Nos igitur fanco Euangelio credentes divinam in primis providétiam veneremur, mentes quocet nostras, qua possumus virtu te, furfum erigamus ab his quae funt caduca et nobisiphis redacti vniamur:quatenus dei maieftatem vbiqet praesentem fideliter intelli gamus, quae cum fit omnino incircumfcrip tibilis, tenet omnia, implet omnia, comple citur omnia, fuperexcedit omnia, & fustinet omnia. SPAN. que ex alia superexcedit, neque ex una parte implet atque ex alia circumplectit: sed circumplectedo implet et impledo circumplectit, sustinendo superexcedido sustinet oia; qui per molem corporis nulg; est, & per incircumscriptibilem substantiam sua nulg; deest, qui oculis carnis nō cernit, q p fi dem i cordis puritate videt. O virtus inexplacabilis, o pietas incōprehēsibilis, o sapientia ieffabilis, o divinitas incircūscriptibilis: q nō partibus cōitas vt corp, nō affectibus dietas vt aia, nō formis subitas vt cetera omnia qua pte facta sunt quae es i oibus et sup oia regēs et gubernās sapientissime vniuersa. His itaq testimōns sacratissime Caesar Maximiliane, satis ( vt reor ) probatũ est, mūdũ hũc vniuersum dei prouidētia gubernari: qui cu sit intellectus purus, simplex, icreatus et sem piternus, oia nouit, oia itelligit, oia ţcognol citatque oipotēs natura cu fit, oia potēs pōt, cui nihil est difficile, nihil impossibile, q tam mirāda creavit potētia sua, i veritate cōstitu it, rōne perfecit, virūte sustinet, bonitāte ils lustratiipsi laus, ipsi honor, ipsi gloriaqvivit et regnat deus gloriosus, & excellus in secu la feculorum. Amen.

Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim.

they were going. What will have to be thought concerning the Christian faith, if God does not care for human affairs? What, finally, concerning the savior of all, our Lord Jesus Christ, except that he will reckon the whole thing an empty fable and a fiction, if there is no providence of God caring for mortal things? Therefore whatever good we do in this life, whatever evil we endure for the love of God, is wholly vain and useless to us, if he has no care at all for us. Let those now see and shudder who deny the providence of God, when they behold the most evil end of their opinion: the despair of all. Therefore let no one, clothed in the vain talk of secular philosophers, train himself to contempt of God; let no one take away the providence of the highest and immutable good; let no one corrupt the dignity of the creator of all things. For all who deny divine providence show themselves both unworthy of and ungrateful for the benefits of the most merciful savior. For it must be firmly believed and in no way doubted that this whole world, visible and invisible, and all things and each thing that are either in heaven or on earth and in the sea, are ruled and governed by divine providence, and that absolutely nothing in the whole universe is alien to his care. For both the crops and all the rest that the earth brings forth, and also storms and the varieties of time and changes of the sky,

The Eighth Question.

by which all things that the earth brings forth grow to their natural maturity, divine providence furnishes and provides for the human race, all things and each thing; not only great things, but also the very least, so much so that not even the very slightest leaf of a tree falls to the ground without the will of almighty God the Father, who created, rules, and cares for them. But if anyone thinks that this so great magnitude of the whole universe cannot be ruled and governed by the eternal God, who alone exists, he is greatly mistaken, and is proved not to know how great is the power of divine might. Indeed, he who was able to bring the whole world from nothing into being is also able most wisely to govern forever what he made. For he knows all things, understands all things, can do all things, who alone, omnipotent, created all things. Therefore we, believing the holy Gospel, should above all venerate divine providence, and lift up our minds, with whatever virtue we can, from these perishable things, and, brought back to our very selves, be united: so that we may faithfully understand the majesty of God present everywhere, which, since it is altogether uncircumscribable, holds all things, fills all things, embraces all things, surpasses all things, and sustains all things. But it does not sustain from one part and

Joh. Trithemius, Abbot of Spanheim.

surpass from another, nor fill from one part and encompass from another; rather, by encompassing it fills, and by filling it encompasses; by sustaining and by surpassing it sustains all things. He is nowhere by the mass of a body, and by his uncircumscribable substance he is lacking nowhere; he is not seen by the eyes of flesh, but he is seen through faith in purity of heart. O unfathomable power, O incomprehensible compassion, O ineffable wisdom, O uncircumscribable divinity: which is not bounded by parts as a body is, not distinguished by affections as a soul is, not subject to forms as all other things are which have been made by you, you who are in all things and above all things, ruling and governing the universe most wisely. Thus by these testimonies, most sacred Caesar Maximilian, it has been sufficiently proved, as I think, that this whole world is governed by the providence of God: he, since he is pure intellect, simple, uncreated, and eternal, knows all things, understands all things, recognizes all things, and because he is omnipotent by nature, he can do all things, for whom nothing is difficult, nothing impossible; who by his power created things so wonderful, established them in truth, perfected them by reason, sustains them by strength, illuminates them by goodness. To him be praise, to him honor, to him glory, who lives and reigns, glorious and exalted God, forever and ever. Amen.

Omnipos tens deus te sua prouidentia dirigat et custo

Eighth Question.

The Author’s Declaration to Caesar.

These are the things, most unconquered Caesar Maximilian, which seemed to me necessary to say in response to the eight questions proposed by Your Majesty. For you wished also to have from me a judgment on these same matters in writing, forming an estimate of me beyond the truth, since in ability I am not to be compared with those whose opinion you heard before me. Let this make me worthy of pardon, if I have said anything less proper: that, set on a journey as a traveler by command of Your Highness, I dictated, as I could, at intervals, whatever occurred to me that should be answered.

But I say from my heart and openly declare that I wish to remain until death a sincere confessor of the Christian faith and in union with the sacrosanct Roman Church. Therefore, if anything either in this little work of mine or in others is held to have been said or written otherwise than she holds, thinks, believes, and teaches, as a true son of obedience I renounce it by the attestation of these presents, and I wish it simply to be and to be held forever revoked.

For this reason, most wise Caesar, I both humbly beg and urgently admonish Your Majesty that, before you cause my responses to come to the knowledge of those for whom they are destined, you cause them to be [approved?] by the judgment of many. For with the utmost care it must be ensured that nothing be proposed to those over whose salvation Your Serenity keeps watch except what is sound, tested, manifest, and lawfully confirmed in the Catholic faith by the opinion of very many wise men.

May almighty God by his providence direct and guard you always to the praise of his name, Maximilian, greatest of emperors. From the city of Neometan, on the tenth day of the month of July, in the Christian year one thousand five hundred eight.
